items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House
that the Joint Committee on the Nationa l Broadband Network Committee from the
Parliament of Australia, led by the Chair, Robe rt Oakeshott, is present in the gallery. I
am sure that members would wish that the delegation be welcomed.
Dotcom Case—Government Communications Security Bureau Actions
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements in relation to Kim Dotcom and the inquiry into the actions of
the Government Communications Security Bureau?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I stand by my full statements in the context
in which they were given.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: When did the Government Communi cations Security Bureau begin
surveillance of Kim Dotcom, and when did it realise it was acting illegally?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the memorandum spells out exactly when that work
began—if the member gives me a moment. It was 16 December 2011, and it ended on
20 January 2012. The Government Communicati ons Security Bureau recognised the
error a few days before it told me—I think it was about 5 to 7 days before it told me.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Who first told him of the Gove rnment Communications Security
Bureau’s illegal surveillance, and approximately what date was that?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It was Monday, 17 September when the Government
Communications Security Bureau came over to advise me there had been an error.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he aware of any involvement by staff from the Department of the
Prime Minister and Cabinet, the SIS, or the National Assessments Bureau in the
Dotcom case; if so, what involvement was that?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not sure about the latter two, the SIS and the National
Assessments Bureau. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet may have been
advised. I do not know that—I would have to  go and check that—but it is possible it
would have known in that period when I was told on Monday the 17th.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did he receive any advice from those agencies in the past 12 months
in relation to the Kim Dotcom case?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Not in relation to this issue. I was informed of that only on 17
September. Whether there was earlier advice on extradition and ot her matters, I am not
sure. I do not think so.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that the ministerial certificate signed by Bill English said that
the Kim Dotcom communication intercepts “w ould likely prejudice the security of New
Zealand”, does he feel he should have been told well before by either Bill English or his
own department?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. It is important to unde rstand what the ministerial
certificate is. The ministerial certificate is essentially a suppression order that was on the
basis of an application by Kim Dotcom’s legal team to release the name of the
5648 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2012
Government Communications Security Bureau’s activity. It is not normal practice for us
to do that. So, because the bureau believed it had acted lawfully, it asked the Acting
Prime Minister to sign the ministerial certific ate, which avoided it having to make that
public statement.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he think he was providing pr oper, democratic oversight of his
agency when he did not receive advice of  the Government Communications Security
Bureau involvement in the Dotcom case in the past 12 months?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. It would be quite inappropriate for me to be involved in a
police raid, and if this member wants to one day be Prime Mini ster and direct the
police—well, that is a pretty interesting way he is going to go. It is—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is sufficient.
Economic Growth—Sustainable Growth and Higher Incomes
2. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What progress is the
Government making to ensure New Zeala nd’s economic growth is sustainable and
supports jobs and higher incomes?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: I can report that the Government is making good progress. Since 2008 we
have been working hard through our br oad-based economic programme to support
business competitiveness in areas such as the tax system, exporting, skills, innovation,
infrastructure, capital markets, and resources. We are seeing good results. The economy
is now growing moderately well, compared with the rest of th e world. A net 57,000
more New Zealanders now have jobs than 2 years ago. Household saving is positive, for
the first time in more than a decade, and total goods and serv ices exported have
increased 15 percent over the last 2 years.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How is the New Zealand economy performing, according to the
latest official gross domestic product statistics?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Statistics New Zealand last week, of course, reported the
gross domestic product data for the June quarter 2012. They showed that the New
Zealand economy grew 0.6 percent in the 3 months to 30 June, and growth for the first 6
months of the year was 1.6 percent. The qua rterly growth was re asonably broad-based,
including agriculture up 4.7 per cent, construction up 3.3 percen t, transport, postal, and
warehousing up 2.7 percent, and manufacturi ng up 0.8 percent. New Zealand’s annual
growth rate of 2.6 percent to June 2012 wa s the highest growth rate since 2007, before
the domestic recession, the Canterbury earthquakes, and the global financial crisis.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How does current progress in building a more productive and
competitive economy compare with the situation in late 2008?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: New Zealanders can be reassured that New Zealand’s
current economic situation is much healthier than it wa s in late 2008. Annual economic
growth is up to 2.6 percent, compared with negative 1.7 percent in December 2008. The
number of people on the unemployment benef it has declined from a peak of 93,000 at
the height of the global financial crisis to 58,000 in July of this year. The household
savings rate is now in positive territory, compared with negative 3 percent in 2008. The
cost of living is flat, with CPI inflation only 1 percent in the year to  June 2012,
compared with 5.1 percent in 2008. The New Z ealand sharemarket is at a 4-year high,
and the average floating mortgage interest rate  is 5.7 percent, compar ed with almost 11
percent in 2008. This all shows that New Z ealand is in pretty good shape, compared
with most other developed countries.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What reports has he seen on new projects that would create
further investment and jobs?
26 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5649

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Minister sees reports ev ery day, and just yesterday he
has seen a report on a project in regard to the Bathurst  Resources escarpment mines
project near Westport. This project would apparently immediately create 225 new jobs
and incomes for workers and families on the West Coast. Unfortunately, it is being held
up by ongoing litigation. Yesterday the Minister saw a report calling for objectors to the
mine to withdraw their appeal s and consider the economic futu re of the West Coast. It
prevailed upon various groups to join the call.  As yet, the Minister has seen no reports
that the Labour Party, the local Labour MP, the Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and
Manufacturing Union, or the Greens will support—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I think the answer has gone on quite long enough.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given the 8 percent decline in exports in the year to August,
announced by Statistics New Zealand just t oday, and Treasury’s prediction that our
external deficit will get even worse, when will he accept that his plan is deficient,
costing exports and jobs, and what is sustainable about that?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would point out to the member that New Zealand’s
exports have grown substantially since his Government left office, and I would point
out that the balance of payments deficit, the external deficit, is considerably lower than
when his Government left office. But I s uppose it is all relative. We know that this
Government is a better economic manager.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: When exports are declining, lo cal businesses are closing, and
thousands of Kiwis are losing their jobs and heading to Australia, why does he sit on his
hands and pretend there is nothing he can do about our inflated currency?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think I hear the printi ng presses cranking up on the
Labour Party side, but I would point out to th e member that he is incorrect. The decline
in manufacturing jobs in New Zealand occurred under the previous Government and
through the global financial cris is. Over the last 2 years the number of manufacturing
jobs has actually grown.
Manufacturing Sector, Jobs—Confidence in Minister for Economic Development
and Effect of Monetary Policy
3. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
have confidence in his Minister for Economic Development in light of the fact that there
have been nearly 40,000 net job losses in th e manufacturing sector in the four years to
June 2012?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I do have confid ence in the Minister
for Economic Development. In fact, having listened to his answers before, I have even
more confidence in him. But I would dispute the member’s use of statistics. According
to the household labour force survey, the number of people employed in the
manufacturing sector has actua lly remained quite steady si nce the beginning of 2009,
fluctuating between 245,000 and 255,000 people depending on the season. In fact, over
the last 2 years employment in manufacturing has actually gone up a little. It is true that
in the past there has been a decline in ma nufacturing jobs in New Zealand. That decline
was shameful, and it happened between 2005 and 2008.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he have confidence in hi s Minister when Statistics New
Zealand figures show that nearly 100 skil led manufacturing workers are leaving this
country every week, annual exports of ma nufactured goods have fallen by nearly $2
billion, or over 12 percent, in the past 4 years, and ma nufacturing’s contribution to
economic output has fallen by nearly $3 billion, or over 9 percent, since 2008?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would dispute some of those f acts, but what I would say is I
would go back to the most rigorous form of measuring employment in the economy and
in relation to the manufacturing sector. That  is the household labour force survey. It
shows that in the time that we have been in office, employment has been pretty static.
5650 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2012
As I say, it has not moved enormously. What I would also say is this Government is
actually trying to build competitiveness in th e manufacturing sector . That is why we
want to have 90-day probationary periods, lower company taxes, reform of research and
development and the likes. And what I notice fr om that party is that time and again it
resists all of those sensible changes to make New Zealand more competitive. So there is
no point in crying wolf here in the Chamber and then going outside—

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is not about the Green
Party’s policies. This was a very straight question to the Prime Minister. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Members should not interject when a point of order is raised.
The member, in asking his question, inserted quite a lot of information into his question
that the Prime Minister has disputed. He is at liberty to do that.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Are companies like Nuplex Industries wrong when they say that
the overvalued dollar is a reason why they are cutting skilled manufacturing jobs; and
are half of the exporters wrong when they sa y that the high and volatile currency is
hurting their business and their sales overseas?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There is no question that the high exchange rate is hurting
some exporters—no question about that. The Government has been, actually, making
the same position quite clear for some time. It is not universal, because against the
Australian dollar, actually, we have been very  competitive. So if we are to follow what
the Labour Party and the Greens want to do, we will start printing money to get the
exchange rate down. They had better go and tell every New Zealand pensioner what
they think of that, because that means high in flation, and that means an erosion of their
savings. If the member wants to be in a Gove rnment that prints money, well, that is an
interesting way to go. It did not work that well for the Germans.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: When will the Government wake up to the fact that most of our
trading partners are taking active steps to devalue their currencies, which is hurting New
Zealand’s exporters and manufacturers, because  they are actively intervening to lower
their currencies, and the f act that the Government’s policy of doing nothing around the
currency is a recipe for more job losse s and a hollowing out of New Zealand’s
manufacturing capacity?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think what is true is that a lot of countries take different
positions when it comes to exchange rate management. So when the member says
countries are doing all sorts of different things to devalue th eir dollar, well, that would
vary depending on who you are lo oking at. In the case of Aust ralia, yes, Australia has
sold Australian dollars and intervened in the exchange rates. In the Reserve Bank’s
latest annual report, if you have a look at it—I urge the member to go and have a look—
have a look at what the market-to-market valu ation of those sales are. When it comes to
China, it happens to have tril lions of dollars in reserves and it is not a capital importer
like New Zealand. If the member wants to go and have a look at Switzerland and see
how successful it has been at defending the Sw iss franc at 1.20 against the euro, he is
welcome to do that. All of these things are voodoo economics that do not work.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table a paper fr om JBWere, from the director of
the investment strategy group, Be rnard Doyle, which states that New Ze aland is out on
its own in running orthodox monetary policy.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table a paper from the IMF chief economist, who
says that the days of simply targeting inflation with monetary policy are over.
26 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5651

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How long does this Government  think it can keep playing by
the rules of 1980s neo-liberalism—the rules so loved of currency speculators—when the
rest of the world is adopti ng modern policies to develop their economies and create
manufacturing jobs?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I say, this is a Government that is working hard to create
manufacturing jobs. I would have strong issue—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, at least we were not the Government that was collapsing
between 2005 and 2008. I would add that I have r eal issue with the characterisation that
the member has that somehow New Zealand’ s monetary policy is out of whack with
that of other countries. Charles Cha uvel chaired the Finance and Expenditure
Committee as part of the old Government  in 2008, and what it found was we had
world’s best practice—world’s best practice. Then there are 20 other countries that have
a very similar approach to inflation targeting as we do, including all the majors. And the
only change that has seriously ever come up with all the reviews—and there has been
four of them, from memory—about monetary policy in New Zealand has been the view
that is held by some peopl e that there should be a committee decidi ng about the
exchange rate, rather than a single person in the form of th e governor. That is it. There
is nothing very odd about the way New Zealand manages monetary policy.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: As the rest of the world m oves beyond our rather outdated
monetary policy framework, and the IMF— the International Monetary Fund—has
recommended moving beyond this simplistic and outdated monetary policy that he has,
does he plan that New Zealand will be the la st Government standing on the planet that
remains a devotee of the neo-liberal religion, or will we adopt modern monetary policy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, I reject the proposition that it is outdated. Secondly, I
think we need to understand what  the member is telling the H ouse, just in case he ever
gets anywhere near an opportunity to im plement things. So he  wants to actively
intervene in the exchange rate to get it down. That is what he is telling New Zealanders.
Well, by the way, while he wants to talk about people who are involved in the currency
market, yep, when I went into the cu rrency market, the US dollar was 320 yen
approximately; today it is 80. The Japanese Government has lost billions and billions
and billions of dollars interv ening the whole way down, and th at pattern is pretty much
the same across every reserve bank. If th e member wants to print money and have
rounds of quantitative easing, which is wh at the Americans and the Europeans are
doing, fair enough, but just unde rstand what the economic imp lication of that is, and
that is basically much higher inflation—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Prime Minister
has been allowed to do this not just to day but on previous days: to suggest that
Opposition parties want to print money.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is not remotely a point of order. The member wishes to
debate an issue. He will sit down. The member will resume hi s seat. That is not
remotely a point of order. The member is trying to use—[ Interruption] The member—
[Interruption] Order! The House will come to order. The member will get control of
himself. The member was seeking to debate  what the Prime Minister had said, by way
of a point of order. That is totally outs ide the Standing Orders, and the member knows
that. I allowed the Prime Minister to go on a little longer because  the question was a
little longer, but I think it was a sufficient answer in the end.
5652 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Speakers have long ruled
that Ministers are not allowed to make up policies for other parties—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is enough of this. Th e Prime Minister did not allege.
The Prime Minister—if the member checks back on the Prime Minister’s answer—said
“if” people want to do things, not that th ey were proposing to do things. The Prime
Minister was quite careful. If I heard him correctly, he said that if the member and
parties want to print money, for example, th is will be the consequence. He was quite
careful in his language.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My recollection is that he
said that if the member got close to the Tr easury benches, then he would. That was his
assertion.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We are not going to take this matter further. The member has a
further supplementary question, should he wish to use it.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Did he or his Minister for Ec onomic Development instruct the
National Party members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee to block an inquiry
into the crisis in manufacturi ng, or is the National Party a ttitude of doing nothing so
deeply imbedded that they just did it for themselves?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I certainly did not instruct them, but this is an
instruction I would like to give: why does this House not get behind and clear away all
of the objections, and let us have the Denni ston mine operating, so those miners on the
West Coast can have a job. But, no, the Green Party is all—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Now the Prime Minister is accusing—[Interruption] Order! I
am on my feet. Now the Prime Minister is accusing another party of certain things.
Business Growth Agenda—Effect on Job Losses
4. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour—New Lynn)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What impact has his Business Growth Agenda had on Nuplex Industries,
Solid Energy, Kawerau and Tiwai Point, a nd how many job cuts have been announced
there in the last two months?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government’s
Business Growth Agenda is undertaking in itiatives in skills,  innovation, natural
resources, capital, infrastructure, and mark et access to assist all New Zealand firms,
including those named by the member, to be more competitive on the world stage, after
our tradable sector declined through the latt er half of the last decade. Of course, the
impact on individual firms at any point in ti me depends on the international state of the
industries in which they operate. Job losses at  the firms mentioned by the member are,
of course, a matter of public record.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Rather than choosing to
answer what was quite a straight question of how many job cuts have been announced
in specific industries or comp anies in the last 2 months, th e Minister chose instead to
give an answer about a previous Govern ment—or an allegation about a previous
Government. If he had that information, he might have sought advice—the question was
on notice—and he could have answered the question that was actually given.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member has some grievance in that the Minister was
asked about how many job cuts have been announced there in the last 2 months. I do not
think saying that it is on th e public record is actually that  informative for the House. I
would ask the Minister, if he has that information, please, to tell the House.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do have some information to hand. My understanding is
that according to media reports the numb ers are 80, 440, 120, and 100. Of course, they
are contrasted with recent announcements on the positive side by companies such as
Xero, Orion Health, Tait Communications, Methanex, The Warehouse—
26 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5653

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. This Minister is trifling
with question time. He deliberately did not pr ovide the answer, despit e the fact that the
question was on notice. He had the informati on provided to him by the ministry, and he
had it at hand. Now he is using—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order! The member is criticising—[Interruption] Order! The
member will resume his seat. The member is criticising the Minister. It is up to the
Speaker to deal with whether or not the Minister has answered the question. I have done
that. I made it clear to the Minister that I was not satisfied with the answer provided to
the question on notice. The Minister did go on to put some context around the answer
and the figures he was giving, and that is not unreasonable,  lest a false impression be
created. Ministers naturally have some li cence to put context around answers, but I
think he had made his point sufficiently.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The way the Minister has
been allowed to answer this  question effectively means that he has two long-winded
answers in respect of one primary question, when he should have had the opportunity to
answer only once and to do it properly then.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I invite the member to read the question carefully. It asks “What
impact has his Business Growth Agenda had on”—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Don’t patronise me.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member read the question carefully, he would realise that
actually it asks an opinion. There is no one who can actually establish any particular
facts about the impact of the Government’s policy on those particular businesses. So the
question seeks an opinion—and I invite the member to reflect on that—and the Minister
gave an opinion in answer. The piece of the qu estion that sought facts was the last part
of the question, and that is why I required the Minister to  advise the House of that
information, because that was the part that s ought the facts. I just invite the member to
think through the question.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. Given that the Minister
has revealed that he does have the informati on to hand, I would invite him, if it is an
official document that he is quoting from, to please table that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member had listened, he would recollect that the Minister was
quoting from newspaper articles.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Why did the Minister say that  the Spring Creek lay-offs are
because “coal prices are on a severe roller coaster around the world”, when Bathurst
Resources’ Denniston mine faces exactly the same  world coal prices, yet he thinks that
that one is economic?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would be happy to explain th at for the member. There are
about two or three reasons why the cost of pr oduction is different at the Denniston field
and, in fact, the Buller field more genera lly, where Denniston and Stockton are both
located. It is because the coal seams are cl ose to the surface and ru n laterally, and also
because they are open-cast mines and, as I understand it, there is not a lot of methane
gas, as distinct from the Grey fields, which are underground mines by definition. They
have very complex geology and are quite difficult. So you have  a production cost at the
Denniston mine that is much lower than th e production cost at th e Spring Creek Mine,
which means that the different mines are much more economic at different prices. I
understand that the private sector investors are more than ready to make their
investment in Denniston, provided, of course, they get the opportunity to do so.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: In light of the answer the Mi nister has just given, could he
please clarify whether he believes that it is more in the national interest to pursue open-
cast coalmining on conservation land or to extract the maximum long-term value from
an existing deep mine shaft at Spring Creek?
5654 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the member is actually recommending that, in lieu
of jobs that would be successful in the open-cast mine, he would prefer the Government
to subsidise an—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s question was fairly clear. What he was asking
the Minister was whether he considers it to be more in the public interest to extract coal
from an open-cast mine on conservation land, if I remember correct ly, compared with
extracting from existing deep-e xtraction—or whatever the co rrect term is—low-impact
mining. It is an opinion he is seeking: which, in the Minister’s opini on, is preferable in
the public interest? That is what the Minister should focus on.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, I believe that it is preferable, in the public interest, to
encourage companies that can have profitable operations to hire workers from the West
Coast to succeed in the mining industry as an alternative to attempting to subsidise
mines that have proved to be not economic at current world prices. [ Interruption]
Absolutely. And if the member does not th ink so, then he needs to take the word
“economic” out of the title “economic development”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe

Parole—Reduction in Unnecessary Hearings
5. IAN McKELVIE (National—Rangitīkei) to the Minister of Justice: What steps
is the Government taking to reduce the st ress on victims caused by unnecessary parole
hearings?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I have today introduced legislation
to implement the Government’s post-election action plan to reduce the number of
unnecessary parole hearings where the offender has little prospect of release. This will
help to reduce the stress caused to victim s by having to attend unnecessary parole
hearings and relive their traumatic experiences when the offender is not genuinely ready
for parole. It is estimated that these cha nges will mean 800 fewer parole hearings each
year.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: How will the changes to the parole regime operate?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The Parole Amendment Bill increases the time between
parole hearings from once every year to once every 2 years, and for those serving
indeterminate sentences or sentences of 10  or more years the maximum time between
parole hearings increases from 3 years to 5 years. Inmates will be encouraged to comply
with offender plans, which will have agreed  goals that aim to reduce the likelihood of
future offending. Hearing dates will be aligned with the completion of milestones. Early
hearings can be held for offenders who achieve early completion of goals.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My point of order is
that it is extraordinarily unusual for a Minister in this Hous e or a member to be accused
26 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5657
of being a liar or to have lied, and for you to do nothing about it from the Chair. That is
extraordinary. I have never seen that befo re. I am asking you: are you going to act in
this case or not?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the point the member raises is an interesting point. The
member may notice that it was its use in a quest ion that I did not object to. I did start to
object to the interjections accusing a member of  lying, but I think that in a question the
language being used is hugely important. If a member were to construct a question that
included the word “lie” or “lied” in a wa y that was outrageous—that accused a member
of outrageous lying or something like that—I  would certainly object, but I think we can
get too precious about some of these thi ngs. One should remember that the Minister
being questioned has the chance to respond. I think it is a very different situation.
Interjections should not be responded to, and that is why I do not accept—members
should desist from interjecting that any memb er lied. I will not tolera te that. But I think
that the wording of questions, so long as the construction is careful and the question
does not make an outrageous assertion, I have not—the same thing came up last week, I
think, from memory, and I did not intervene. Part of the reason for that is that the
Minister has the chance to respond in answer, but I would intervene if the construction
of the question was such that it, in my view, was outrageous.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I cannot put my finger
on this, because it is outside of the Standing Orders, but if a member of this House is
not in a position to defend himself, it surely behoves somebody in this House, including,
perhaps, you, to do that for him, if it is capable to be done, which is my point.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept that it is an interesting point that the member raises. But I
invite him to reflect on the fact that where a question is being asked, and as long as the
language is moderate, the Minister being que stioned has the chance to defend the other
Minister, if it is involving a nother Minister, and the memb er may note that the right
honourable Prime Minister has done that. He has defended the Minister at some length.
So it is an interesting issue. I certainly do not want to hear me mbers accusing other
members across the House of lying. I do not want to hear that at all. I do not want to
hear accusations like that being made even in  debate. In question time, as long as the
construction is careful and moderate, I am certainly prepared to listen to the advice of
the House on it, but I do not want to keep intervening all the time. To me, the important
thing is the construction of the question and whether it is making an outrageous
assertion. I mean, there seems to be, wher e there are questions around the accuracy of
information—certainly, in this particular do cument, there is a quest ion here; there seem
to be some arguments around whether or not the information in it is accurate. To me, to
pussyfoot too much around the la nguage, I think, is just bei ng excessively pedantic, as
long as the use of the language is not outrageous.

Child Protection—Role of Social Workers
8. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland) to the Minister for Social Development:
What difference do social workers make in  protecting our most vulnerable children
from abuse and neglect?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Around 1,300 Child,
Youth and Family social workers deal with more than 400 notifi cations of abuse and
neglect every day in New Zealand. Social workers often bear the brunt of criticism
when things go wrong, but the fact is they do the job because they care, and every day
they do the best they can to protect New Zealand. Ultimately, they save children’s lives.
26 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5659
Today is National Social Workers Day, and I think it is our chance to thank them for the
job they do on behalf of our children and most vulnerable families.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: How is the Government supporting more services to families who
might benefit from working with a social worker?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: As I have said, we know th at social workers can and do
make a difference with our families, and particularly those who are most vulnerable.
That is why this Government has provide d extra funding to increase the number of
front-line social workers. There will be 80 new front-line social workers with 16 new
supervisors, and more than half of that num ber are already at work now. We have also
announced an extra 149 full-time social work ers in our low-decile schools. Most of
them are on board, working and making a difference.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: What have been some of the recent data trends of New Zealand’s child
abuse statistics?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: It has been quite interesting. In the most recent Child,
Youth and Family figures we have seen the first drop in substantiated cases of abuse for
at least the last 8 years—granted, by only 4 pe rcent in findings of substantiated abuse.
However, notifications have gone up—those that required further action—so follow-up
went up, but actual, substantiated cases have  gone down. I think it is too soon to tell
whether that will continue, whether it is a trend,  but it would be fair to say that it is, if
nothing else, encouraging. Als o, Child, Youth and Family met or exceeded 97 percent
of its targets in the year 2011-12, including notification response, compared with in
2005-06, where it was meeting only about 42 percent. So, I mean, it has doubled its
response time and we are seeing fewer substantiated cases of abuse.

Fuel Efficiency—Heavy Vehicle Fuel Efficiency Programme
12. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney)  to the Minister of Energy and

items.speaker: Resources
items.text: What progress has the Government ma de on promoting fuel efficiency in
heavy road vehicles?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Last week I launched
the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority’s Heavy Vehicle Fuel Efficiency
programme, which will help fleet operators cut their fuel bills by 10 percent on average,
with some achieving savings of up to 20 per cent. If all heavy ve hicle fleets in New
Zealand reduce their fuel bills by 10 per cent, nationwide savi ngs could total $130
million each year. This initiative will help ou r vehicle fleet to become significantly
more fuel efficient, with the wider economy and the environment reaping the rewards.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: How important is the heavy fleet sector for fuel efficiency?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Transport makes up around 40 percent of New Zealand’s
energy use, and New Zealand’s heavy vehicle fleet of 127,000 makes up about a fifth of
this. At an individual company level, a fleet of 25 trucks using 1 million litres of fuel
annually, which is not unusual, could realistically make savings of $130,000 per annum.
With a very competitive industry and with small profit margins, these savings are very
significant to the bottom line of companies.

1. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First) to the Member in charge of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primar y Function of Bank) Amendment Bill :
What will the Reserve Bank of New Zeal and (Amending Primary Function of Bank)
Amendment Bill enable the Reserve Bank to do to address the overvalued dollar?
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand (Amending Primary Func tion of Bank) Amendment Bill) : Our bill would
enable the Reserve Bank to use a range of tools to address the problem of an overvalued
exchange rate. The most direct way, of course, is by intervention. The last time the bank
used its powers to intervene was in 2007 when the dollar reached US80c. The bank
intervened, the dollar came down, and the bank made a profit of $411 million.
However, the bank would have to also make  better use of supplementary stabilisation
instruments, such as, for example, reserve ra tios or mortgage intere st levies and other
counter-inflationary measures intended to take pressure off the overvalued exchange
rate.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill—Effect on Export Sector
3. BARBARA STEWART (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primar y Function of Bank) Amendment Bill :
What is the importance of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary
Function of Bank) Amendment Bill to New Zealand exporters?
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill): It is beginning to
look like it is the only hope th at they have currently got. Fo r us to be internationally
competitive, the critical thing is the level of  the dollar. Exporters have been struggling
with a chronically overvalued exchange rate for years. You have got closures, you have
got cutbacks, you have got all sorts of peopl e losing their jobs, you have got relocations
offshore, and you have got 54,000 now leaving every year because we have failed to act
in the national interest of an export- dependent economy. I hope before 17 October
enough of rural New Zealand will have persua ded these recalcitrants to do their duty by
their country.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I move, That the
House take note of miscellaneous business . Meanwhile, back in the real world, the
economy is growing 2.5 percent larger than it wa s this time last year and there are
57,000 more jobs in the New Zealand economy than 2 years ago. Household saving is
positive for the first time in more than a d ecade, and total goods and services exports
have increased dramatically over the last c ouple of years, and all without getting the
printing presses out and trying to print mone y, like the desperate approach suggested by
Mr Peters, who, incidentally, never came up with it in all the time he has been in
various Governments over the 20,000-odd years he has been in Parliament. Nobody has
come up with a proposal today that is a so lution. The New Zealand economy is actually
doing pretty well compared with most parts of the developed world—not as well as we
would like. There are upsides and there are downsides. There are some people who are
doing well and there are some people who are struggling—we understand that—because
of the global financial crisis and what has been happening around the world and what
has been happening in our own country in terms of the Christchurch earthquakes.
This week was a tough week down the West  Coast, with the news that the Spring
Creek Mine is losing money and is uneconomic to keep open at current coal prices. That
is very difficult. But there could be an upsid e. Just up the coast th ere is another mining
project that is ready to go, which is economi c at current coal prices. There are private
investors who want to invest in a new mine up the coast on the Denniston Plateau. They
have consents, but they also have appeal s against those consents. Roughly the same
number of jobs could be crea ted at this new project as ar e being lost in the uneconomic
underground mine in Spring Creek. That is the opportunity.
So yesterday I called on the objectors to just once—just once, in a special case—
withdraw their objections, to allow this mine  to go ahead; to withdraw their objections
and to assist. I suggested th at the Labour Party, supposedly in favour of jobs, the Green
Party, supposedly in favour of jobs—and it wants to have a select committee hearing on
manufacturing, which is, of course, including coal—and the Amalgamated Engineering,
Printing and Manufacturing Union join me in  that call. There has been a deafening
silence. The union popped its head up and sa id: “Oh, actually, we support the Bathurst
Resources mining application.” It popped its head up. I went back to it and said does
26 Sep 2012 General Debate 5667
that mean it supports my call for the objec tions to be withdrawn, and there was a
deafening silence from the union. It was not on the side of making the call to have those
objections withdrawn.
Where was the local MP? Where was one  Damien O’Connor? Damien O’Connor
was nowhere. I asked, and there was no sign of any comment from Damien O’Connor
about the importance of withdrawing the a ppeals and getting these jobs going on the
Coast. And what about the leadership of  the Labour Party, the members who were on
the steps of Parliament yesterday—on the steps of Parliament talking to the miners—but
who have been deafening in their silence on calling for the appeals to be withdrawn?
They have not done it. And then there is the Green Party, whic h has cried crocodile
tears about manufacturing jobs in the country. Where were Mr Hague and his colleagues
when I suggested they talk to their mates in the environmental movement and suggest
the appeals be withdrawn? They were absolu tely nowhere. Their silence is deafening. It
is absolutely appalling that on the one hand they say that they have got an interest in
jobs, but on the other hand they will keep really quiet—really quiet—when it comes to
actually supporting this. Then there is Anne tte King, who has absolu tely no interest in
it. So it is a very straightforward exerci se. I would welcome the support of the Green
Party and the Labour Party. The local MP, alongside the National Party—

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would welcome the member taking a call and saying that
he too calls on the appellants to withdraw their objections to the Bathurst Resources
mine, and if he is prepared to do that, I would welcome that. That would be fantastic.
But, basically, at the moment the La bour Party, the Greens, the Amalgamated
Engineering, Printing and Ma nufacturing Union, and, of c ourse, the environmentalists
are all very, very quiet about  viable jobs on the West Coast. This Government is
focused on building competitive opportunities for companies to grow, and once again
we learnt this week that the Opposition is not.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: The Spring Creek Mine should remain open. It is going,
instead, to be mothballed. It is going to be mothballed because of this Government’s
asset sales agenda. As the documents betw een these Ministers and the Solid Energy
board clearly demonstrate, the board has been instructed to prepare the company for sale
to maximise the share price. That is why Solid Energy is being denied the opportunity
to exercise its normal functions of managing through price fluctuations.
The asset sales agenda of this Govern ment is going to leave the Government
accounts over $100 million a year worse off. It is going to increase electricity prices, it
is going to lose strategic control of important New Zealand assets, and it is going to lose
sovereignty for New Zealanders. It is going to cost the jobs and the livelihoods of all of
5668 General Debate 26 Sep 2012
those people who will lose their jobs and their families, and it is going to cause a terrific
economic impact to my home community of Gr eymouth. For all those jobs that will be
directly lost, there will be a knock-on effect, and probably there will be two jobs lost for
every one directly lost. Those will be felt in ancillary in dustries, by contractors, by
retailers, and in schools. The impact will be profound.
The profits from coalmining currently all l eave the Coast. In Mr Joyce’s preferred
option of Denniston and the Bathurst Resources mine, they will not only leave the
Coast, they will leave the country. But the wa ges spent by those coalminers in our local
economy are an important input into our local economy. The reality is that these miners,
the miners who will lose their jobs as a result of the Government’s actions, will
tomorrow or the day after, instead, be on a plane to Australia, some of whom having
come to the West Coast—
Simon O’Connor: They could be at the mine down the road.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: —from halfway round the world in order to take up jobs only
recently offered to them by Solid Energy. It does not have to be that way—the
Government is quite right. It could reverse its decision. It could reverse its agenda of
asset sales. It could hold out the hand and assist the mi ners of Spring Creek and the
local mine management, who came up with a to tally viable plan t o, in fact, keep the
mine open. But the Government has chosen not  to do that. The Green Party’s policy is,
indeed, for no new coalmines, but our policy is  to have existing mines continue to be
open. That is because there needs to be time for transition—transition for industries to
be able to move to new technologies that do not require coal, and also transition in local
economies so that there are jobs to replace these ones that will be lost.
Minister Joyce has, I believe, interfered in proper judicial process by calling on those
who have a legitimate case before the cour ts to withdraw it. I believe that is
inappropriate. But Mr Joyce’s red herring is pa rticularly objectionable, because it is a
bit galling to be lectured on job creation by  someone who has presid ed over the loss of
almost 40,000 manufacturing jobs in this c ountry. His suggestion of  moving these jobs
to Denniston actually misunderstands the na ture of coalmining. These are specialist
skills, and most of the jobs are not readily transferable between one and the other. But,
also, rather than being just up the Coast, De nniston is not in our community at all; it is
150 kilometres away. So he is expecting that  these miners will uproot their families
again and move on to Westport. Then, after that one is exhausted, maybe it will mean
moving on to the next one, and that might be Canvastown.
His expectation is that this labour force will follow the booms and the asset bubbles
throughout the country. That reminds me of the 19 th century economy of this country
and of the West Coast. The really galling thing is this: we have a Minister for Economic
Development whose entire vision for economic development appears to be more of old
19th century industries, and who has no grasp wh atsoever of the need  to transition the
West Coast economy and, indeed, the New Zealand economy to a new one that actually
creates high value, quality jobs.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I just want to start today by
talking a little bit about th e fact that this is Childre n of Prisoners Week. PILLARS,
which is a charity that supports prisoners’ fam ilies, has released the results of a 2-year
study into children of prisoners, which s how that 23,000 New Zealand children have a
parent who is in prison—23,000. They are seve n times more likely, those children, to
end up in prison. The National Government has set a target of reducing reoffending by
25 percent by 2017. That includes addressing a ddiction and increasing education and
skills training. The most important thing for those children, though, is facilitating the
employment of that parent back into their communities. That is what is going to make
the biggest difference for those 23,000 ch ildren. Work is happening around New
26 Sep 2012 General Debate 5669
Zealand, but I want to particularly emphasise that huge work is being done around skills
and employment in Christchurch so that the prisoners can help wi th the rebuilding of
Christchurch.
I note in a New Zealand Herald  article today that the New Zealand Herald has
actually gone out and had a look at the Mt Ed en Corrections Facility, to look at its
groundbreaking family visiting rooms, with th eir brightly coloured play areas and
kiddie packs of food that parents can buy. Thes e new ideas are all in place in a prison
that is run by private enterprise. It is run by Serco. The Opposition parties are against
Serco, and they are against having new a nd innovative ideas brought into our prison
service throughout New Zealand.
But we want to talk about jobs here today. On that same note, I want to make the
point that for the new prison that is to be built at Wiri the first sod was turned last week.
We have got a consortium called Secure Future, which is a public-private partnership. It
is going to build, maintain, and run that prison, Wiri Prison, in South Auckland, and
save New Zealand taxpayers $170 million. That c ontract with Secure Future will save
New Zealand taxpayers $170 million. Do you think the Opposition supports it? No. The
Opposition is against it. It is quite happy for New Zealand taxpayers to pay another
$170 million to build the prison, because it does  not support private enterprise getting
involved.
This project in Wiri will create a thousand construction jobs over—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: —the next 2 years—a thous and construction jobs. Do you
think the Opposition parties are supporting that ? No, of course they are not. Of course

project, this company, Fletcher Buildi ng, will be spending $25 million a month—$25
million a month. Do you think the Opposition is supporting that? Oh, of course it is not.
It is against this too. When it is constructed, the new Wiri Prison will have almost 300
permanent jobs.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How many is that?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: 300 permanent jobs. Do you think the Opposition is
supporting that? No, of course  not. Anything that this Government puts up to create
jobs, the Opposition is against. When I was up there last week I heard that a local
contractor is providing cater ing on site for the thousand workers. They are talking
between 30 and 50 jobs from the local comm unity providing the on-site catering. Do
you think the Opposition parties are in favour of this?

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Let’s have a guess.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Have a guess. Do you think they are in favour of this
project? No, they are against this project from beginning to end.
This National Government is focused, first of  all, on making sure the prisoners get a
good education, get rid of their addiction, and get back into our communities and
working. Secondly, we are about creating a brighter future—a  brighter future. Do you
think the Opposition parties are supporting that? Absolutely not.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Well, there we have it, the
Government’s new economic growth agenda: a prison on every corner. That is the
answer from Anne Tolley. If we just built a prison on every corner in New Zealand, we
would solve the problems. It is another great economic growth strategy from the
Government.
The Government’s handling of the Kim Do tcom case and the involvement of the

House to endure the statement that we have  to believe that our spy agency is so
incompetent that it could not even use Google and google “Kim Dotcom residency”. If
it did, it would come up with 6 million hits. There are 6 million pages on Kim Dotcom’s
residency, but the Government Communications  Security Bureau, we are told, was not
even able to identify that he was a resident. This is on the back of  an operation that has
been so badly botched. There were illegal  search warrants. We  now know there was
illegal surveillance. It has been described as Keystone Kops, but if we are to believe just
how incompetent these people are, it actually should be called “John Key’s stoned
cops”, because that is how badly it is doing it.
The ringmaster of this circus is John Key. Once upon a time, the casual, relaxed John
Key was who the public wanted to see, but when it comes to having oversight of our
security agencies it is not a place for the casual, relaxed John Key. Mr Key is the sole
democratic check on how these security agen cies operate. He is the person charged on
our behalf as New Zealanders with oversight  of these security agencies, and he has
failed. Along with his deputy leader, Bill English, he has failed to uphold acceptable
standards of oversight over organisations that have extraordinary powers.
Many New Zealanders will accept that we need  in our society the ability to ensure
that we monitor those who would act ag ainst our country. I think it is highly
questionable in this case whether it meets that test, but people in New Zealand will
accept that. They will accept that, on the basis that there is some kind of oversight—that
there is somebody in Government who is ma king sure that these agencies are acting
appropriately. That is the j ob of the Prime Minister, and he has failed to do that. He
should be held to account for the actions of this agency. He cannot keep coming down
to this House and saying he is not responsib le. He is the Minister  responsible for the
Government Communications Security Bureau, and he is responsible for the actions of
this agency that has behaved so incompetently in this situation.
The Prime Minister claims that he has had 15 meetings with the Government
Communications Security Bureau this year —15 meetings. He says that Kim Dotcom
did not come up in any of those meetings. I find it incredible that a situation like this has
not been raised with the Prime Minister in th at role or in the many other roles that he
has. He could not even tell us today whether or not his own department had been
involved. That defies belief, and it speak s of a Prime Minister  whose once casual,
relaxed attitude is now seeing him missing in action on critical issues for this country.
The National Government is now so totally distracted and embroiled in its own
scandals—scandals of its own making—with John Banks and the Kim Dotcom affair
that it is neglecting the core j ob that it has, and that is to help New Zealanders stay in
work. Time after time in this House we get the excuses from Steven Joyce and others,
but the reality is that hundreds and, in f act, thousands of New Zealanders are losing
their jobs every day as this Government stands by and says that it can do nothing. In the
last year, 54,000 people went to Australia, a nd this Government stands by and says it
can do nothing.
Once upon a time, this Government gave some  hope to New Zealanders. It said there
would be a brighter future. Mr  Key said there would be high er standards of Ministers.
There is no brighter future. There is no bri ghter future for the families of the hundreds
of people who are losing their jobs at the Spring Creek Mi ne and in Kawerau and right
around New Zealand. There is no  hope for those people. Th is Government has let New
Zealanders down. It promised big. It said that  it would build a brighter future for New
Zealanders. The only brighter future New Zeal anders are finding is in Australia at the
moment. This Government is missing in ac tion, and totally distracted in its own
scandals. It has no idea how to create jobs. It has no idea how to grow the economy, and
it should go.
26 Sep 2012 General Debate 5671

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: There is something
slightly ironic and cynical about the Labour Party and the Green Party railing against
people going to Australia. Incidentally, they are going to Australia to work in the
mining and the oil and gas industries, and a ll the while the Labour Party and the Green
Party are stopping mining and oil and gas ex ploration in New Zealand. But there is
something more ironic and cynical than that, and that is that, a pparently, the Labour
Party and the Green Party think it is OK for miners to work at the Spring Creek Mine
getting coal out of the ground, but they  oppose miners going up the road a few
kilometres and mining on the Denniston Plateau.
So what I want to ask Damien O’Connor, w ho is the member of Parliament for the
West Coast, is this: is he for mining on th e West Coast, or is he against mining on the
West Coast? He seems to support mining at  the Spring Creek Mine , but not mining on
the Denniston Plateau.
Hon Damien O’Connor: I seek leave of the House to answer that question raised by
the member.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member seeking leave to make a personal explanation?
Hon Damien O’Connor: I am. I am seeking leave to make a personal explanation.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to make a pe rsonal explanati on. Is there any
objection? There is no objection.
Hon Damien O’Connor: Let me be very clear here. I have always supported mining
on the West Coast, and I will, but it must be done in an environmentally responsible
way, and it must follow due process. This National Government has—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is nothing to do w ith a personal explanation, and I
caution the member. The House grants member s leave to make personal explanations
because members feel deeply about certain issues. It should not be abused.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: So here is the thing. The La bour Party and the Green Party
support mining in some areas of the West Co ast, such as the Spring Creek Mine, but,
apparently, oppose mining in ot her parts of the West Coas t, such as the Denniston
Plateau. In fact, what they do is they get out  a little map of New Z ealand and they draw
lines where they want to support mining and where they want to oppose it, and it all
depends where the votes are. There is nothi ng principled about it —nothing principled
about it at all.
But what is cynical—and iron ic, really—is that it points to the bigger picture, which
is that they wax lyrical in  this House week after wee k, and up and down the country,
about New Zealanders going over to Australia. In fact, I get it in th e electorate that I
represent, in Whangarei, and Mike Sabin ge ts it in Northland. Ma ny Northlanders have
put up their hands and they have said “Look, we are going to Australia to work in the oil
and gas and mining industry. We are going to get excellent salaries, and, by the way, we
are not going to be actually  mining. We’re builders, and we’re plumbers, and we’re
electricians, and we’re cooks, and we’re truck drivers, but because of the mining and oil
and gas industry over in Perth, in Australi a, it is happening there and we will go over
there and get jobs.”
Hone Harawira is crying that all his relative s, or at least half of them, are going to
Australia to work in the mining industry, and he is crying that th e other half of his
relatives are staying in New Zealand and th ey are in the dole queue, but he will not
support mining and oil and gas exploration in Northland. The Labour Party and the
Green Party will not support oil and gas exploration and mining in New Zealand.
The funny thing about it is that in Tara naki—our only region where oil and gas
production occurs—you have got about 4,500 j obs directly involved there, about
another 1,500 jobs indirectly , and an average wage of about $80,000 a year, and it has
happened for a hundred years. The other 15 or 16 regions of New Zealand over the last
5672 General Debate 26 Sep 2012
hundred years have never heard a problem co me out of Taranaki. They have always
understood that there is dairy farming, and tourism, and oil and gas exploration in
Taranaki—never a problem.
But the minute that the National Party and all those in Taranaki who support oil and
gas exploration—it has been so  successful—say “Why don’t we extend this to some of
the other regions in New Zealand? There ar e about 16 or 17 othe rs. We have been
successful in Taranaki for over 100 years. Why don’t we extend it to some other regions
of New Zealand, such as off the Otago coast,  the East Coast of the North Island, or
Northland?”, apparently, according to the Labour Party, and the Green Party, and Hone
Harawira, the sky is going to fall on our head.
So it has been successful in Taranaki fo r 100 years with never a whimper, alongside
dairy farming and tourism, but somehow we cannot repeat it elsewhere in the country.
So I question Damien O’Connor and the Labour Party, and ask why, when we have a
formula that has been so successful in one  of our most highly paid regions in New
Zealand, Taranaki, we cannot repeat it elsewhere in the country.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The Labour Party position on mining has never
been unclear, and it has always been cons istent. Outside of schedule 4 areas like
national parks, we have always said it ought  to be done on a case  by case basis. We
approve of mining, but people have to get a consent under the Resource Management
Act or the Crown Minerals Act. The law has not been changed by National in that
regard in any great way, a nd our position has not change d since we were last in
Government, when we spent $25 million of taxpayers’ money helping to get data to
make it a little bit less ris ky for the oil and gas industry.  So although we  do not think
mining is the whole answer to New Zealand’ s economic problems, we admit that it is
part of it, and we do not oppose it outside  of schedule 4 areas. The National Party
people should do a bit of research.
Why is it that those members are rattling on about it? It is because they do not want
to talk about the economy, and they do not want  to talk about jobs, because, in fact, all
they do is focus on one political disaster afte r another. Let us list them this year. Well,
we have had the Dotcom one recently. That  has been addressed by Grant Robertson. I
will not go into that any further. Go back a little while and we ha ve the Government’s
centrepiece of its Budget: improving student outcomes by increasing class sizes. What a
nonsense that was, and the Government had to back down. It spent 2 months defending
that ridiculous policy when it should have been doing things to save people’s jobs.
Go back a little bit further, like just a month before that, and we had Nick Smith
falling on his sword because of the debacle at  ACC, which saw not only the Minister
resign but also the board resign. The chair wa s, effectively, aske d to resign, and the
board followed him because that was so mismanaged. That was another month when the
Government was not managing the economy.
Go back a little bit further and you have th e problems with the teapot tape and the
Prime Minister’s scandals around that. We have got the Prime Minister’s scandals
around his electorate chairper son being appointed to New Zealand On Air, called the
Broadcasting Commission.
Simon O’Connor: Talk about policy, not people.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: What was that?
Simon O’Connor: Stick to policy.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: That is what the Government is embroiled in every day,
and in the last month we have had John Ba nks. What should the Government be doing?
It should be doing what it can do to help  stop this shedding of jobs—160,000 people
have gone to Australia since this Government was elected. That is more than the
population of the city I come from. Dunedin has about 100,000 people—160,000 people
26 Sep 2012 General Debate 5673
have gone just to Australia. That is not the rest  of the world; that is  just Australia. They
are record numbers every month because th ere are no job prospects here. Despite the
fact that a lot of the unempl oyed have given up and gone to Au stralia, we have still got
far higher unemployment now than when this Government came into office. The safety
valve, as Bill English describes the Aust ralian economy, has kept New Zealand’s
unemployment lower than it would otherwise be, because those people have gone to get
jobs in Australia.
What could the Government do? It could save some of these export jobs by doing
what a responsible Government  would do: back Winston’s bi ll to a select committee,
and change the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act so that we do not give primacy to the
targeting of inflation ahead of other aspects of economic management. The IMF says we
should do that. Nobel Laureates like Joseph Stiglitz say we should do that. Most of the
Governments around the world have moved on from—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Joseph Stalin?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: —giving inflation targeting primacy. Joseph Stalin. That is
what we get: Joseph Stalin. That  is just like Steven Joyce.  If anyone comes out with an
alternative economic policy, it is economic voodoo, it is snake oil remedy, or, from Mr
Finlayson, it is Joseph Stalin when you talk about Nobel Laureate Jo seph Stiglitz, who
is a free marketeer, to a certain extent. He  is Joseph Stalin, according to the National
Party. These guys are so out of touch that they have had more people go to Australia
than live in Dunedin, and they say “Oh, we don’t need to change anything.” They do not
need to change anything.
This Government is embroiled in its own controversies. It is not properly managing
the economy. We are losing export jobs that will be very, very hard to get back, and, as
a consequence, New Zealanders are disa ppointed. They have given up on waiting for
the brighter future from the National Govern ment, and they are voting with their feet
and going to Australia instead.

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Can I just take up the challenge
of that member who has just sat down, David Parker, when he said that we do not want
to talk about jobs, because I do want to talk about jobs because jobs matter. Businesses
create jobs, and businesses need policy settings that encourage jobs and encourage
growth—policy settings around jobs—policy settings that members opposite say no to.
Why do they say no to it? Why is it that th eir policies over there on that side of the
House are not about creating j obs or helping jobs or enha ncing job growth? What they
are about is cutting and reducing jobs.
Last week we celebrated Women’s Suffrag e Day. It is a great day in the New
Zealand calendar. We celebrated Women’s Suffrage Day, and what was the very first
action that the Labour Party did on that day? It  had the first reading of a bill that would
have immediately cut the j obs—3,350 jobs—of women in New Zealand. It would have
cut the jobs of 3,350 women in New Zealand. Th at is how much it th inks of jobs, and
that is how much it thinks of women. By raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour in
an unrealistic and unsustainable manner, that  would have reduced jobs and cut jobs by
5,500. Why do those members say no? Why do th ey say no to any job-enhancing policy
that we put up? They just say no.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: The Minister understands the minimum wage. She’s had the
advice. It doesn’t cost that.

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Mr Clark does not understand. His first big job in this
Parliament was to introduce a bill that would have lost 3,350 jobs for women, and its
first reading was on, symbolically, Women’s Su ffrage Day. That is the shame of that
member and that is the legacy of that member. On Women’s Suffrage Day 3,350 jobs
would have been lost—lost, just like that, by a stroke of a pen.
5674 General Debate 26 Sep 2012
We have the 90-day trial, which research has shown is responsible for the creation of

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: —13,000 jobs. That was when it related to only small
and medium sized enterprises—i.e. busine sses with under 20 peopl e. It created 13,000
jobs. Since then it has been expanded to all businesses. Imagine how many jobs that will
be responsible for. And what do those memb ers say? They say no. They say no to a 90-
day trial. It is part of thei r policy to repeal it—13,000 jobs, ju st like that, all gone. They
say no, and they talk about jobs!
My colleague Minister Tolley spoke a bout prisoners helping the rebuild of
Christchurch. Well, the 90-day trial is an ideal tool for businesses to have the
confidence to actually employ those prisoners to help in that rebuild. What will the
Labour Party do? It will say no.
That 90-day trial is encouraging businesses to take on more staff. It has been used by
many businesses. It has shown that the major ity of employers keep their staff once the
trial is over, so that people who are on th e fringes—they might be young, they might be
older, they might be wome n, but David Clark does not like them, or they might be
prisoners—are given the opportunity to get th eir feet on the employment ladder and get
a job. It is a fantastic policy that, embarrassi ngly, Labour will repeal . It is a policy that
is working really well in these tough econom ic times, and Labour will repeal it because
it wants to say no to all job-enhancing policies. I think it is a shame.
Those members sit there smugly, thinking that  they have got the answers. All they
want to do is say no. They stop things. They would have had The Hobbit go overseas.
The Hobbit haters would have had The Hobbit go overseas. Since then we have had
Avatar over here—1,500 new jobs—and we are l ooking at a new sequel. Is that not
fantastic for our movie market? More jobs—what do they say? They say no.
We have some great policy settings for cr eating jobs and for en couraging businesses
to actually expand. Successful businesses, by expanding, will take on more staff, which
means more jobs, and that must be good for our economy. We are about creating jobs;
they have policies that say no.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I want to talk about a group of New Zealanders who
have already been mentioned this afternoon by none other than our corrections Minister,
Anne Tolley. This is a group of people who ha ve variously been called the forgotten
victims of crime, the orphans of justice,  and the unseen victims of the prison boom. I
want to talk about the 20,000-plus young New Zealanders who have one of their parents
currently in prison. On any given day, we have over 20,000 young people in this
situation, and we are doing very little to m eet their current needs—their very severe,
present-day needs—and we are doing arguably ev en less to try to secure for them a
better and safer future, and to steer them aw ay from following the line of that parent
who may be incarcerated.
The Minister’s attention might have been brought to the New Zealand Herald article.
I do not know whether before seeing that arti cle she knew that this week is actually
Children of Prisoners Week, and it is a good time to acknowledge the NGOs. There are
groups like PILLARS—Ng ā Pou Whakahou—that work cons tantly and very hard and
very effectively to try to provide services to  these neglected kids, and to try to mitigate
some of the suffering of, and burdens on, those kids and their families.
Before I talk more about that, I must respond directly, though, to some of the
comments the Minister made ear lier. She was very thrilled to announce that she is
saving $170 million on building this prison at  Wiri. I am really fascinated by the
arithmetic there. The Minister has told us th at the total cost will be  in the order of $840
million. Serco, the private contractor that will run the prison, has proudly announced to
26 Sep 2012 General Debate 5675
the British London Stock Exchange that it expects revenues of $30 million a year over
25 years. My arithmetic gives that a figur e of $750 million of revenue, leaving about
$90 million to construct that prison. We know that the average cost of a prison is around
$400,000 per bed, allowing that by the scale of the prison you can re duce that cost. Are
we seriously expected to believe that th at prison is to be built for $90 million? We
would love the Minister to table the cont ract. Show us the numbers. Be a little
transparent about what is actually going on in  Wiri and the real cost to New Zealand—
not only the social but the financial cost.
The Minister was thrilled to note that  her beloved private prison has been
acknowledged as treating better the families and children who are visiting inmates. This
Government has had within its power for 4 l ong years the ability to intervene in terms
of the conditions facing visitors to prisons. Is it beyond its collective wit to realise that
the application of some paint, some toy boxes, some colouring books and crayons for
children could actually break some of the f ear and some of the trauma these kids
experience every time they walk into those very forbidding, very hostile places? I have
visited the prisons, and I would encourage mo re members of the Government to do so.
Visiting rooms have rows of plastic chairs bolted to the floor, with no privacy and no
provision for children. There is no distractio n for them while their parents endeavour to
maintain a relationship with one imprisoned partner. We know that on average for a
couple where one of them enters prison, typically the man, the relationship might
survive for some 18 months. Anybody sentenced to  more than that is likely to come out
to find their relationship is gone. The children  have lost their fath er—or, indeed, their
mother—and the mother has lost her partner and an income earner. This is an
intolerable situation and it is unacceptable that the NGOs are doing a great deal more
than Government agencies to actually reme dy the situation that is confronting these
young people.
There are major differences in visiting polic ies from one prison to another. Why is it
that a partner visiting a prisoner in one pl ace has a very differe nt experience from
another? The very least we could do is improve the situation when these young people
and their parents are visiting inmates. We do very little to protect the health and well-
being of children of prisoners. We do very little to support their partners. We know that
their educational outcomes will be way belo w optimal. We know that they will suffer
serious health and psychological health traumas. We know through all the evidence that
comes to us that these are some of the most disadvantaged young people in New
Zealand. We are doing very little for them. It is shameful. We need to do more. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: The Chinese have a curs e expressing the hope that
one may live in interesting times. These are interesting times not just in New Zealand
but in every country in the developed a nd developing world. As the IMF Managing
Director, Christine Lagarde, said recently, the global economy is experiencing a
widespread decline of conf idence as problems mount in  the eurozone and beyond. Ms
Lagarde said further that policy makers ever ywhere must maintain a crisis management
mode as risks increase. The IMF is pressi ng Governments around the world to step up
their responses as both advanced and emerging economies show troubling slow-downs.
Here in New Zealand the Government is  resolutely focused on guiding our economy
through these troubled times. We are reducing our exposure to overseas debt markets as
much as possible, while still continuing to cushion vulnerable New Zealanders from the
harshest edges of the ongoing financial crisis . We have got lots to be happy about and
thankful for. Our GDP grew 0.6 percent in the 3 months to  30 June. This took annual
growth to 2.6 percent, the highest rate since 2007. The first half of this year has seen
GDP growing at 1.6 percent. New Zealand’s economy is performing better than those of
Japan, the US, the UK, France, and Germany, and growth in this last quarter is on a par
5676 General Debate 26 Sep 2012
with Australia’s. We cannot hope to influe nce the external events that impact upon our
small country and relatively tiny economy. What we can do, what we must do, and what
we will do is continue to concentrate on our wide-ranging economic programme. It is an
economic programme that will increase New Zealand’s long-term competitiveness and
give our businesses the best chance of succeeding.
We focus on growth that is sustainable and built on higher savings and earnings,
rather than ever-increasing consumpti on and debt. New Zealand’s households and
businesses are recognising that the cheap fi nance feeding frenzy facilitated under the
supervised neglect regime of the last La bour Government is unsustainable, untenable,
and, ultimately, a road to nowhere other than economic and social stagnation. The
message is getting through. New Zealanders  are saving more, with a positive household
savings rate for the first time in a d ecade. The ANZ bank’s fancifully named
truckometer, an index based on traffic volumes and selected roads around New Zealand,
suggests increasingly robust growth in the fourth quarter of this year.
This Government understands that sust ainable economic growth that creates
permanent, worthwhile jobs is best ach ieved by building a competitive economy that
allows businesses to trade successfully with the rest of the world. There are 60,000
more jobs in New Zealand than 2 years a go. New Zealand needs more jobs and higher-
paying jobs. Why? Because jobs give people income to support their families. Jobs give
people money to pay taxes to pay for public services. And more and more higher-paying
