items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I have several matters to raise
in this call, but I just want to pick up the point that the Minister for Arts, Culture and
Heritage was just raising. The question of whether or not there should be a Treaty clause
in the bill was deal t with in discussion at the Tr ansport and Industrial Relations
Committee, and there certainly was some disc ussion about whether that was needed or
required in this bill.
One of the important things to  note, and it is one of the i ssues that I certainly myself
raised in the select committee, is that the bill’s title does include in it the National War
Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill, and that is a reference, by the inclusion of
the word “Pukeahu” in here, to the way in which that land is known to, particularly, the
Taranaki Whānui and those who are part of the Po rt Nicholson Block Settlement Trust.
I do believe it is incumbent on this House to  have some recognition of the important
role that the Taranaki Wh ānui have played in this particul ar area. We were given in the
select committee an excellent submission on be half of the Port Nicholson trust by Liz
Mellish, and she did go through some of the hi story of this area and the significance of
the area for the Taranaki Whānui.
What the committee did was make specific recognition in the commentary on the bill
around the important role that the Taranaki Wh ānui and the Port Nicholson trust have
played in this area and, certainl y, our belief that they must continue to play that role.
They are involved in a number of places in th is bill in their role as a landowner. In
particular, the land immediately beside the Carillon is owned jointly, I think, by Massey
University and the Port Nicholson settlement  trust. So they do ha ve a significant role.
They should have a significant, ongoing role in  the way that this park is developed, and
I certainly hope that is something that th e Government will pick up, given the support
that the trust has given over the years fo r the war memorial, and obviously now, we
hope, for the park. So on this side of the Ch amber we would certainly like to note that
an important part of this bill is the recognition of the role of the Port Nicholson trust and
the Taranaki Whānui, and they certainly will have a role in a number of areas.
Now that we are taking the debate on this bill as one question, I just wanted to pick
up several of the key changes that have been made throughout the bill. In a sense for
me, as the local member where this park wi ll be built, I have had concern throughout
this process to make sure that, yes, we do ev erything that we can to  see it built in time
26 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5697
for the 100th commemoration of Gallipoli in April 2015, and that is an important thing.
This park has widespread s upport in the electorate that I represent, and everyone who
sat through the select committee process would have seen, with a couple of exceptions,
that the submissions that came before us st rongly supported getting this park built, and
strongly supported getting it built in as quick a time as possible.
As I said in my second reading speech, this  is not ideal legislation. I do not like the
fact that the Government is  passing empowering legislati on that goes over the top of
other Acts of Parliament, but from time to  time there will be sufficiently nationally
significant projects that require  this, for whatever reason, a nd I will not rehearse those
arguments again around how it is that we find ourselves in this position. We on this side
of the Chamber feel more activity could have happened in the last 3 years, but it has not.
We are now in the position of wanting to s upport the bill and get it through. But we do,
in that context, have to make sure the community is as involved as it possibly can be.
The significant changes that I want to highl ight are, in particul ar, the expansion of
the role and the number of meetings of th e community forum established under clause
36 of the bill. The two organisations that the committee has included are the owners of
the Mount Cook Police Barracks and the Tasman  Garden Body Corporate, which is on
the other side of the intersection of Buckle Street and Tasman Street from the barracks.
It is important that the local residents have a role in the de velopment of this park, and a
significant change we have made in the committee is to include that community forum
having a role in the final design of the park. That is important to the people of the
Mount Cook community. They want this park to be in their community and they
strongly support the reasons for it, but it will change their community and in the process
of it being developed it will severely disrup t their community. Therefore, they deserve
the chance to have a role in its development.
So we are pleased that the community foru m is being expanded. We are pleased that
the number of meetings has gone up to at leas t three, and I would ur ge the Minister to
make sure that that community forum meets as often as is needed  and that there are
other opportunities. The Minister and I discussed this in th e second reading. There have
already been some community meetings. I wa nt there to be more. There was actually
another community meeting last night, whic h discussed this in some depth—the Mt
Victoria Residents Association annual general meeting, whic h the Minister in the chair
was to have attended, but did not. He was not there. He will be thrilled to learn that a
fake Mr Finlayson attended the meeting and offered a number of positions on his behalf.
I am sure that he would warmly endorse those positions. There is a great deal of
community interest in this bill, and I think that if we  can see the community forum
playing that key and important role, member s on this side of the Chamber would be
reassured.
The other area that I want to raise is th e whole question around Orders in Council.
Certainly, going into this bill, this was so mething that we on the Labour side of the
Chamber wanted to ensure—that is, there were  the right protections  in place so that
Orders in Council are seen as wh at they should be, which is as  a last resort in the event
that the extensive provisions contained in this bill are not enough to achieve the goals of
the bill. That may occur from time to time, but if it does, the process of Orders in
Council is such that we need to put all the protections possible in place to make sure
that they are used only in that way.
That is what new clause 24(4) is about. It is the last resort clause. It mentions the fact
that the Minister can go down the path of  Orders in Council only if they have
“considered all other reasonably practicab le ways relevant to the particular
circumstances to achieve the purpose specif ied …” in the legisl ation. The key phrase
there is “all other reasonably practicable ways ”. What that is signa lling to the Minister
5698 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 26 Sep 2012
under this Act is that they can use the Orde rs in Council process only when it is
absolutely necessary, as an absolute last resort. I would hope that there will not be a
great deal of need for that, because the schedules of this bill outline a very extensive set
of regulation powers and consen ting powers that are given under this Act. But if it is
needed, that is the last resort clause.
The other part of that Orders in Council pr ocess is making sure that this Parliament
has a role if that is done. The Minister has wisely set up a review panel so that any
Orders in Council must go to that review panel. What we wanted and what I am pleased
to say is now in this bill is that there will be a report back to this House every 6 months
about what that review panel has done, what Orders in Council have come up. That is
important. It will allow members of Parliament to know what is happening.
The other change that we made there was an extension around the disallowance
process. This is actually to give members of  Parliament the right to be able to oppose
any of these Orders in Counc il, to actually give some proper time for that to be
considered, so we have extended that out to 12 sitting days from the 6 sitting days that
was originally in the bill.
From our point of view on this side of the Chamber, we are strong supporters of this
memorial park. We believe that it will give New Zealanders the kind of place to reflect
on the sacrifices people have made in war, to reflect on the impact of war. It will give
green space to Wellington where it much need s it. It will be a place that Wellingtonians
will be proud of. In terms of this legislation, we have to make sure that in giving the
power to make this park happen, we also protect the rights of Wellingtonians and of
New Zealanders more generally. I believe the changes that the committee has made
make that happen, and on that basis we are happy to be supporting this.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I would like to pick up where my
colleague Grant Robertson has left off, and sa y that there is widesp read support for this
bill, the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. When Grant
Robertson was talking about how important it is  to his electorate, because it actually is
in his electorate, I need to reinforce the fact  that I think it is important across the whole
of Wellington. But, even greater than that, because it is a National War Memorial Park,
it is of significance to all New Zealanders, a nd I think it was made so by the return of
the Unknown Warrior and the burial of the Unknown Warrior in that spot, signifying for
all New Zealanders a place where we honour and we commemorate the loss of many
lives during many wars.
There was widespread support during the hear ing of this bill, including from the
community but also from the Wellington City Council, and I think th at was significant.
My understanding is that Celia Wade-B rown, the Green Mayor of Wellington,
supported this bill. In fact, there were only two councillors  who opposed it. I think that
probably shows the depth of feeling here in We llington for this park and for the
completion of this park.
I think it was unfortunate th at during the select committ ee stage, although concerns
were raised about the process, the Greens did take the position that they would oppose
the bill. They want the park, but they oppose the bill. It seemed to me that that was a bit
like having a bob each way—you could say you wanted the park, but you were not
prepared to vote for it. I think it would have been really tremendous if this House could
have had unanimous support for this bill. I understand the concerns about the process,
but when I look at the work that was done in  the select committee and the changes that
were made to make the bill, in terms of th e Orders in Council, as robust as possible and
as transparent as possible, the Order in Council would be considered only as a last resort
and all other reasonably practicable ways mu st be considered before an Order in
Council. I think that the work that was done in terms of th e review panel and extending
26 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5699
the consideration up to 12 sitti ng days helped to strengthen the bill. I do not think there
are many members in the House who want to see us not use proper process, but every
now and then, in my experience, an occasion does arise where you can have a process
that is not ideal but will be for the greater good. This was one of those cases when there
was a need, I think, for the Parl iament to say that this is a very good thing to do. This is
good for Wellington, but it is also good for New Zealand.
Something that did concern me was that we  could not get support across the House.
It is no good saying you support it but then saying let it be built sometime in the future.
There is a date required for the building of this, and we could argue, and we did argue in
the select committee stage, that  it ought to have been starte d sooner, that it ought to be
finished in time for 2015 without the need fo r this legislation. The reality is it will not.
We do want it for the 100 th celebration commemoration of Gallipoli, and to do that, it
may require that there has to be some acti on taken to speed up the construction of this
park.
It is also of interest to me that in the original propos als and discussions with the
former Mayor of Wellington, there was an idea that, in fact, the council would like to
enhance Taranaki Street, which comes off Buckle Street, perhaps with a tree-lined
avenue so that there would be a wide avenue  that leads into the park. I would hope that
at some time in the future that could be considered by the council. In fact, although you
would still be driving up that avenue, it woul d kind of blend into the whole idea of the
National War Memorial. I am not sure where the council sits on that now, but it was
something that Kerry Prendergast was pretty keen on.
I think the work, as I said, done at the select committee has strengthened this bill. We
strongly support it. We would like to see it passed as soon as possible.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: My contributions to the

I suppose what I wanted to say is that having come to this debate with that

feels they have a stake and an interest in what goes on in Wellington and want to have a

kōrero e p ēnei ana: “All persons exercising func tions and powers under this Act must
take into account the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi)”. Me kī,
kei te whai t ēnei wāhanga o te ture i ēnei kupu k ōrero tonu, i ērā i roto i te Resource
Management Act 1991. Me k ī, i tangohia mai ai t ērā wāhanga o te Resource
Management Act, ka m ētia atu ki t ēnei pire n ō reira, ēhara i te mea kai te noho
taupatupatu ngā kupu. Kāo. E ōrite ana ngā korero, e rite tonu ana ng ā kōrero o roto i te
Resource Management Act me tēnei o ngā kaupapa.
He aha te take o t ērā? Me k ī, kia whai w āhi te ao Māori i roto i ng ā nekeneke
whakahaere, mē kī, o tēnei o ngā kaupapa. Kua tae mai wētahi kōrero, me kī, o te hunga
kāinga, o te mana whenua o t ēnei kāinga, tēnei tā Grant Robertson e k ōrero nei, kai te
hiahia rātou ki te whai wāhi i roto i ngā kōrero e pā ana ki te wāhi nei; kā tahi. Ka rua, e
hia kē nei ngā momo iwi, ng ā iwi kaua ko te tangata whenua engari ko ng ā iwi kua eke
mai ki roto o Te Whanga-nui-a-Tara. Kai te p īrangi rātou kia whai w āhi i roto i t ēnei o
ngā kaupapa anō hoki. Nō reira, mā tēnei o ngā kupu kōrero ka whai wāhi, tuatahi, ko te
mana whenua, tuarua, me k ī, ko ngā iwi kua haere mai ki te Whare i Te Whanga-nui-a-
Tara.
Ka toru, n āku i whakap ā atu m ātou ki te Port Nicholson Settlement Trust me te
Wellington Tenths Trust ahakoa, kai raro r ātou, t ētahi w āhanga, me k ī, o te Port
Nicholson Trust i te raruraru, hoi an ō, waiho tērā ki te taha. I t ōna mutunga mai, kua k ī
mai ngā rōpū e rua nei, ar ā, ngā rūnanga, me k ī, e rua nei, kia tautoko Te P āti Māori i
tēnei huarahi, ar ā, te whakatakoto i ētahi kupu tautoko, ko te noho a ng ā iwi k āinga ki
roto i ng ā nekeneke o t ēnei pire. Ēhara i te mea, he nui te Supplementary Order Paper,
he pakupaku noa iho. He ruarua noa iho ng ā kupu ēngari, ko tōna tūturutanga inā kē, te
nui o te āhuatanga o ng ā kupu nei. Kua kite atu t ātou i t ēnei r ārangi k ōrero i roto i
wētahi atu pire, ā, ka mutu, he aha tōna pūtake tuatahi? He whakanui i te āhuatanga o Te
Tiriti o Waitangi i roto i ng ā ture o te motu, ka tahi, i t ōna t ūturutanga, ko t ērā o ng ā
hiahia o ng ā mana whenua, o ng ā iwi M āori, kia whai w āhi i roto i ng ā korero, i roto i
ngā whakahaere, i roto i ngā whakaritenga e pā ana, me kī, i tēnei wā tonu nei, ki tēnei o
ngā wāhi, ki tēnei o ngā Whare ki Pukeāhua, ka rua.
Nō reira, koi nei te wh ānui, te wh āroa o te Supplementary Order Paper me te
tūmanako ia, ka tautoko mai ng ā taha o te Whare i t ēnei o ng ā huarahi. Ēhara i te mea
he uaua, he m āmā noa iho t ōna p ūtake ēngari, in ā kē ng ā wh āinga ka puta men ā ka
tāpirihia atu tēnei Supplementary Order Paper ki te wh ānuitanga o tēnei pire. Koi nei te
īnoi atu ki te Whare kia āta aro mai ki t ēnei o ngā kaupapa, ka mutu, ki  te Minita tonu,
tērā pea, ka whai w āhi a ia ki te tautoko i t ēnei o ng ā wāhanga. Nō reira, huri noa kia
ora tātau.
[Greetings, Mr Chair, and to us debating this bill that h onours those who went
overseas. I want to outline  some views that the M āori Party has on this bill and about
the Supplementary Order Paper 131 that was submitted to the Minister for Arts, Culture
and Heritage today. Firstly, we support the wishes and hopes of the House on the
parliamentary complex that this stand as a memorial, shall we say, for those who fought
and fell overseas. We have no problems or concerns with that issue. We are hearing
concerns from some about how fast the bill is moving and not, shall we say, following
due process, but it is not as though there are many problems with that.
The main reason for rising to take the call was to put forth our position on the
Supplementary Order Paper, and to have a new 3A section created for it. What would it
be for? To have a statement about the Treaty of Waitangi included in it. The wording
will go like this: “All persons  exercising functions and powe rs under this Act must take
26 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5703
into account the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi)”. This makes
it consistent with the actual wording in the Resource Management Act 1991. In fact, it
was taken directly from that section of the Resource Management Act to include here.
Therefore, there is no confli ct in the wording—none. They are the exact words in the
Resource Management Act and this one of the Acts.
Why is that? Let us say, so that M āoridom can participate in the mechanisms of this
one of the Acts. Word has come to me from  locals, from local tribes, like what Grant
Robertson states, that they w ant to participate in the cons ultations relating to this
place; that is the first one. The second is that there are several other ethnic groups and
tribes, quite apart from the home people, who have settled in Wellington over the years.
They too would like an opportunity to participate in this Act as  well. Therefore, it is by
this statement that the local tribe and other tribes or ethnic groups who have come to
the House in Wellington be able to participate.
The third point is that I have been in c ontact with the Port Nicholson Settlement
Trust and Wellington Tenths Trust on beha lf of our party. Despite the problems among
them, namely the Port Nicholson Trust part—but we will leave that situation there. At
the end of it all, these two enti ties have endorsed the move by the M āori Party to
include references to the Treaty of Waitangi  in this bill to ensure local tribes’
involvement. It is not as  though the Supplementary Order Paper is a huge one; it is
quite a small one really. There are only a few words involved, however the depth and
significance of these words are immense. We have seen these words in other bills, but in
the end, what is its first prio rity? In the first instance it is  to magnify the Treaty of
Waitangi in the laws of the country and to authe nticate it. Secondly, it is to satisfy the
wishes of local tribes and Māoridom to participate in discussions and arrangements, let
us say, in the first instance about this place and this House of Pukeāhua.
So that is the extent and long-standing natur e of this Supplementary Order Paper.
The hope is that all sides of the House support it. It is not as though it is a difficult thing
to consider; furthermore, there are numerous benefits that would accrue should this
Supplementary Order Paper be added to the br oader part of this bill.  This, then, is the
plea to the House that it really take due note of this bill, and finally, to the Minister, that
he finds favour with this of the provisions. So to us throughout, thank you.]

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I want to take just a brief call
to finish my contribution in the Committee stage of the National War Memorial Park
(Pukeahu) Empowering Bill, because we are taking this as one question. I just want to
note one area that I did not mention in my prev ious couple of calls, and that is that there
are extensive schedules to this bill. It is important to note what they do and what they
involve, and it picks up some of what Te Ururoa Flavell just mentioned. A number of
different organisations and people are drawn into how this park will develop through the
schedules, and that includes the Port Nichol son Block Settlement Trust and the wider

the point for the member that within the schedules there are a number of places in which
they have a role in the development of the park.
One of the more curious matters that arose during the select committee process was
around the maps that are in schedule 10 of the b ill. I just want to note for the record that
although these maps are indicative of what w ill happen, they are not, of course, exactly
to the exact centimetre, in terms of scale, of what will happen.
One thing I want to note about these maps is that this is the place in which local

5704 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 26 Sep 2012
that they will now be driving a little furthe r before veering left and heading up towards

I know that the officials and Mr Finlayson are working on that engagement

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I will take just a brief call on the National War
Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill, as we are only 5 minutes away from the
dinner break. I spoke in the H ouse on this bill yesterday and on the merits of this park,
and certainly New Zealand First is very supportive of this as the National War
Memorial Park. However, today I would like to  bring to the attent ion of the House an
aspect that we also must not forget, and th at is the welfare and the interests of our
veterans.
It is all very well, as a nation, spending $12 million on this park, and it is a wonderful
thing that we are doing to commemorate the many hundreds of thousands who have
given of their lives for this country over the last century, but we still have a lot of
veterans alive today in this country who ar e suffering and are in need of care from the
State. Many are suffering from all sorts of ailments as a result of  their service to the
country, and in many cases they are in a perilous state. Many are getting very, very aged
and frail. So although it is wonderful that the veterans are supportive and are very
appreciative of the fact that this war memorial park is an honour to them in respect of
the living and of those who have fallen on be half of our country, I think it is also
important at this time that we remember that we still have a duty of care to the many,
many veterans who are still with us today. There are bot h old and young veterans who
are in various states of ill health and have problems that are as a result of having gone
overseas on behalf of their country, fighting in various theatres of war, and who now, as
a result, have medical problems, ailments, and the like, as do their family members as
well.
If I could say just one thing, it is that I hope all parties in th is Chamber can also
remember that we should not just be build ing monuments and parks;  we should also be
very much remembering those who are here today. I think that would be an even greater
honour to those who have fallen. Those who have fallen would always want to ensure
that their friends and comrades who are still  living, but suffering as  a result, are taken
care of by this country. I implore and say to the Minister and the Government that,

although there was a war pensi ons review 2 years ago by th e Law Commission, there is
still a lot of outstanding work to be done on that for the War Pensions Act review, and
there is a lot of work to be done in terms of veterans’ affairs. I just hope that between all
of us in this House, all MPs, we can get ar ound this and get in behind what is a physical
stone structure and also a green park, but at the same time put a lot of emphasis—

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am pleased to take a short call at the Committee
stage of the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. May I start by
saying, as I believe my colleagues have at othe r stages of this bill , that the Green Party
is strongly in support of the objective of a National War Memorial Park at Pukeahu, and
that we share the desire, if it would be possibl e, for this to be completed in time for the
Gallipoli centenary and Anzac Day 2015. We belie ve the proposed memorial park will
provide New Zealanders and overseas visitors with a dedicated space in which to reflect
on the loss and sacrifice of lif e in numerous armed conflicts, to pay respect to the dead,
to contemplate the causes for which those conflicts were fought, and also, importantly,
to consider the cause of peace and to refl ect on how future armed conflicts may be
avoided. It also would provide a haven of much-needed green space within the busy
environs of the capital city.
However, we have found ourselves unable to  continue to support the bill, despite
some of the amendments made at the sele ct committee, because of our fundamental
concerns about the extraordinary powers granted by the legislation.
But I would like, at this point, to acknowledge the work of the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee, which I sat in on for the duration of this bill. I think the
first point to note about that select committee process is that it was an extremely
constrained one and very challenging for th e committee to do its work within the time
frame, and, indeed, for the officials to do th e work within the tim e frame allocated, and
that is part of the concern that we have with this bill. But within those constraints I think
the committee did work well, and I enjoyed my experience on the committee.
I am pleased to say that some of the amendments that the committee has made are
minor improvements to the bill—for exampl e, the adoption of changes recommended
by the Regulations Review Committee, which somewhat improve the transparency and
accountability of the Order in Council proce ss by making sure that Ministers have to
explore every other available option releva nt before moving to making Orders in
Council, and, indeed, to beef up and improve the community forum and improve the
number of times that that community forum is delegated to meet.
So there are some changes the committ ee made that do improve the bill, but,
unfortunately, the fundamental concerns that  the Green Party has with the legislation
remain, despite those changes, because not  only does it remove and replace normal
planning processes, which limits the abilit y for the public and key stakeholders to
participate in decision making about the park, but also it grants the ability for the Crown
to make wide-reaching changes by Order in  Council without the usual parliamentary
scrutiny. We in the Green Party are very concerned about the pr ecedent that these
powers set about the primacy of the rule of law in New Zealand. We heard at the
committee a particularly interesting subm ission from the Legislation Advisory
Committee, which expressed concern that if we put aside the rule of law in the case of
this legislation, in order to expedite what  is indeed a noble goal in the National War
Memorial Park, it will become easier to put it aside again for future legislation. Indeed,
5706 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 26 Sep 2012
we believe that that is what  has already taken place with the fact that we have this
legislation, this extraordinary legislation, in front of the House in the first place.
This legislation is based upon the provi sions provided for in response to the
Canterbury earthquake, which wa s a national emergency. We were told at the time that
those provisions for Order in Council and t hose extraordinary powers granted to the
executive by that legislation were necessary only because it was a response to a drastic
national emergency and were so extraordinar y that we need not be concerned about
their use elsewhere. Yet here, not so very long after that, we  have a piece of legislation
effecting those same powers for what is ab solutely not a national emergency. In fact, it
has been foreseen for a very long time that we might want to commemorate the
centenary of Gallipoli in some appropriate way in 2015, and indeed the plans for this
particular memorial park have been in place for a long time. The urgency with which
this legislation has been a ddressed was necessary only because of a decision to halt
funding for the project—a long pa use in its progress—and then a very rapid decision to
advance with it after all. That is not good process.

26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5707
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE (TOBACCO PRODUCTS—BUDGET MEASURES)
In Committee
Part 1  Excise and excise-equivalent duties on tobacco products

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Thank you for the
opportunity to speak on Part 1 of the Cu stoms and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget
Measures) Amendment Bill. What Part 1 of this bill does is allow for four substantive
10 percent increases in the excise duty on tobacco products. This is being done in the
name of harm reduction, to reduce the harm caused by tobacco smoking in New
Zealand. It is being done in a wa y that, as has been discussed in earlier readings of this
bill, actually follows the evidence for using tax increases or price increases to reduce the
prevalence of smoking in a much stronger way than previous increases have done. That
is because it allows for four successive increases in price. What the evidence tells us is
that each time we have a price increase, then associated with that is a spike in quitting
activity, whether that be people contacting or ganisations like Quitline, whether that be
acquiring nicotine replacement treatments—or  a whole host of quitting activities. We
also know that as a result of those quitti ng activities many people do remain tobacco-
free as a result of those quit attempts, although the nature of addiction being what it is,
many people also go back to using cigarettes and other tobacco products after those quit
attempts. But what we also know is that ther e is a brief period of activity after each
increase, which then tails off, and we retu rn to a steady level of tobacco consumption,
albeit hopefully lower than what it was pr evious to the increase. So with these
consecutive increases, what we should then see are consecutive periods of quitting
activity from people who are currently using tobacco, and they will assist in progressing
New Zealand towards the goal of being smoke-free by 2025.
But it is important to also note that this, being a tax increase, does generate additional
revenue for the Government. Treasury estimat es that this legisl ation will raise an
additional $528 million for the Government over the next 4 years. What I found
interesting is that for a pi ece of legislation that the Government has proposed in the
name of health and in the name of harm reduction, this bill went not to the Health
Committee but to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and, in fact, the reports, the
regulatory impact statement, and the departmental report were prepared by Treasury not
by the Ministry of Health. That is more appropriate for a bill that is designed purely as a
revenue-gathering exercise, rather than an exercise in improving the health and well-
being of New Zealanders. The chair of the Health Committee is looking at me a little bit
perplexed and is perhaps concerned that I might be suggesting this is not a health
measure and is, in fact, just a revenue-gat hering exercise. I do not believe that, Mr
Hutchison. I do know that this is being do ne with the best intentions—the right
intentions. But it does also  raise money for the Govern ment, and it comes at an
interesting time.
It is interesting that the G overnment has chosen now, rather  than the year before, or
the year before that, or even going back to the days when National was in Opposition, to
support a bill like this. Of course, what we  do know is that the Government has been
having a lot of trouble raising the revenue it requires, because the economy is so
sluggish at the moment. So this does have a positive benefit for a Government that is
having a lot of trouble in its economic manage ment at the moment. It is having some
difficult getting the economy moving along. This measure does have an additional
benefit for the Government in that it does raise some more  revenue. That, of course,
then begs the question of what the Government  ought to do with that revenue. It is true
that there are a number of m easures that the Government could be undertaking in order
5708 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
to further tackle the prevalence of tobacco smoking, and to further advance New
Zealand towards that goal of being smoke-f ree by 2025, that, in fact, would be a very,
very good use for this money.
There is a range of things that the money being raised from the sale of tobacco could
be used for, whether it be through GS T, and whether it be through excise tax.
Obviously, there is the expend iture on the treatment of peop le who have diseases that
are related to smoking. There is , of course, tobacco. We know that tobacco is related to
all the big four killers—not just the big four k illers, but the big four creators of cost in
the health system—cardiovascular disease, di abetes, respiratory disease, and, of course,
cancer, which is well documented. Of course, a lot of the money raised from the duties,
excises, and GST on tobacco products needs to be used to pay for those treatments. It
also needs to be used to boost the health promotion activities that the Government ought
to be carrying out in order to convince people to not start smoking in the first place, and
also to quit.
Of course, what we know is that one of the other initiatives that has a strong evidence
base behind it is social marketing, which encourages people to quit. In fact, if that social
marketing was aligned to these tax increases, it would have an additional effect in
encouraging people to give up smoking. Unfortuna tely, the truth is that the Government
has reduced its spending on those social marketing initiatives, despite the fact that it is
increasing its revenue from the sale of tobacco.
There is a third area that needs to be cove red as well, and this, perhaps, does not get
as much consideration or debate in the public . That is the fact th at people who do get a
disease that is related to smoking of tobacco products are less productive. They are less
able to work. They, therefore, pay less ta x. So there is a burden on the New Zealand
taxpayer because of that loss of productivity that is related to tobacco smoking as well,
and that ought to be covered off by the money raised through tobacco taxation too.
There is an important question that the Government ought to answer: what is it
planning to do with this a dditional money? Is this ju st making up for its economic
failures? Is this just a way of filling the hole created by its unaffordable income tax cuts,
as we have seen with the range of other levies and costs placed on the New Zealand
taxpayer through indirect taxation that does not come through income tax, and making
up for that loss of revenue from income tax, or will this money be used to get us closer
to that goal of making New Zealand smoke-f ree by 2025? I would appreciate an answer
from the Minister in the ch air, the Minister of Ener gy and Resources, on those
questions, because I think they are important questions.
People do accept that increasing the revenue that the Government takes from tobacco
is an effective method for reducing the harm caused by tobacco, but it does have an
impact, particularly on low-income people w ho are addicted to tobacco products. And I
note that Treasury actually acknowledges in its regulatory impact statement that the
nature of addiction is that even if a product beco mes more unaffordable, people may
continue using it because they are addicted to  it, and they do not necessarily make what
most people might consider a logical decision about their use of that product. So given
that that is the situation, it would be fair  for the Government to do more in terms of
supporting people to quit, encouraging people to  quit, and making sure that the types of
replacement therapies, social  marketing, and all the othe r things that go along with
encouraging less use of tobacco amongst the population of New Zealand would all be
good things to be funded out of this money. So I do ask the Minister, if he feels inclined
to get to his feet, to answer those questions on Part 1 of this bill.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I rise to take a call on behalf of New Zealand
First on the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures) Amendment
Bill. We spoke on this bill yesterday, and it is back in the House again today. Some of
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5709
you will recall that yesterday, on behalf of New Zealand First, I expressed our concerns
that this would be simply a tax take. As we have heard, $528 million over 4 years—a
huge amount of money, over half a billion dollars—will be going into Government
coffers. We certainly are hopeful, and expect that it will be the case,  that a significant
amount of the funding that comes out of this  measure will go into  the required health
measures to actually help with the reduction of smoking in our country.
While I was sitting in for the Rt Hon Winston Peters on the Finance and Expenditure
Committee on a few of the days, we did actu ally flesh out some of the unknown factors
in all this. One of the ones that somewhat su rprised me was that this always does refer
to New Zealand becoming smoke-free by 2025. So  there is the feeling out there that
there will be no more smoking in another 12 or so  years. In actual fact, the definition of
“smoke-free” from the officials was that by that  stage it would mean that where there is
currently something like 16 percent of New Zealanders who smoke, it would be slashed
by about a third, down to something like 5 or 6 percent of New Zealanders who smoke,
which would still leave 50,000 or 60,000 people in this country smoking. So it cannot
really be called smoke-free, because even at 2025 there will still be 50,000-plus people
who are defined as being smokers in this country.
In that situation, it is  perhaps a little bit more level ling in terms of what the true
situation is. But we do also have a situat ion with foreign tour ists. Of course, New
Zealand is promoting itself heavily in markets like China, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, and all
through the Asian countries, and that is a potentially huge gr owth market for tourism to
New Zealand. Of course, they do have a high percentage of smokers coming from many
of those Asian countries. So, again, New Zealand will always have a situation where we
cannot become 100 percent smoke-free, because if we are going to expect to have
several million tourists a year coming to th is country, and a signi ficant chunk of those
tourists are coming out of ma ny of those countries where th ere is still a reasonably high
level of smoking, then that will not be the case. If we were to turn it off flatly, many of
those tourists simply would not bother co ming to New Zealand, and that would be a
huge problem.
I think we have to be a little bit realistic he re. It is an admirable aim, but what we are
basically saying is that we are trying to cut the rate of smoking of domestic residents in
this country, of New Zealanders  in this country, by about a third, from 15 or 16 percent
down to about 5 percent. At that point in time, that would significantly reduce by more
than 100,000 people the amount of people w ho are smoking. In that respect, I would
certainly hope that if you multiply those 100,000 people out across the health system
and consider the effects of smoking—we have  the chairman of the Health Committee
here, Dr Hutchison, and I know that this is a subject dear to hi s heart—over the next
decade and the next 12 years, if that can be significantly reduced in terms of the effects
on their health, the reduction in what happens in terms of their health, the extension of
their lives, and increasing their life expectancy, then that certainly is a good thing.
It did worry me a little bit, too, that this  bill was being seen only by the Finance and
Expenditure Committee, and it seemed to be being seen only in terms of dollars, but I
certainly hope that Dr Hutchison and the Health Committee will take it on board.
Actually, I hope that his committee monitors this. I have known Dr Hutchison for many,
many years, because he was a doctor in Maira ngi Bay and I used to go to his practice. I
know how he is committed to good health. So I certainly hope, Dr Hutchison, that you
will follow this through and that you are fighting with your Minister of Finance, Bill
English, for an allocation of increased funding—the increased funding that comes out of
these taxes year on year, 10 pe rcent year on year—for the n ecessary health projects to
reduce smoking. Thank you.
5710 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: I am pleased to contribute to this Committee
stage debate on the Customs and Exci se (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures)
Amendment Bill. Yesterday when I spoke on th is bill, I talked about the numbers of
New Zealanders who die from smoking-related illnesses or from passive smoking—the
inhalation of other people’s smoke. It sits at somewhere around 4,500 to 5,000 people
per year who die prematurely because of the effects of tobacco. So I applaud the
Government’s efforts to make tobacco harder to purchase, which is what this bill will
do.
This bill amends the Customs and Excise  Act—and I am speaking to Part 1—to
increase by 10 percent the excise on tobacco  every year for the next 4 years. So,
effective from 1 January 2013, 1 January  2014, 1 January 2015, and 1 January 2016,
there will be a 10 percent increase in the excise on tobacco. That will help to put the
product itself further out of the reach of young people, and that is an important step.
But I have to go back to some points I ma de yesterday, and which my colleague Iain
Lees-Galloway has made again this evening, th at if this were truly a health measure
with health-related objectives in mind, pe rhaps the first objective in the regulatory
impact statement written by Treasury would not read: “This analysis assesses options to
increase tobacco excise to help achieve  the objectives of responsibly managing
Government’s finances to achieve its fiscal  strategy goals;”. Objective number one: to
achieve its fiscal strategy goals. This is a ta x grab. This is not about health. Had it been
about health, it would have come to the Health Committee. It might have been
introduced by the health Minister. It is in th e name of an associate health Minister, the
Hon Tariana Turia, but even she was not pr esent. She was clearly involved in some
other activity and was not able to move the second reading of the bill herself, so it fell to
the Hon Chester Borrows.
There are a number of people in the Na tional Government who will be hoodwinked
tonight into getting up a nd saying how good this will be for the health of New
Zealanders. I expect Dr Hutchison, the chair of the Health Committee, to be one such
hoodwinked. I am anticipating Dr Hutchison’s speech. In fact, I will be seriously
disappointed if Dr Hutchison does not get up and tell us how good this is for people’s
health. He used to be a doctor—he used to be  a doctor. So I would expect him to get up
and say that.
I am very pleased, for health reasons—and so is the Labour Pa rty—to support this
bill, but the thing I find missing in Part 1 of this bill, which is the part currently under
discussion, is the thing that might persua de me that the Government had health
measures in mind and not simply managing th e Government’s finances to achieve its
fiscal strategy goals. Certainly, secondly, it does have “achieving the Government’s
goal of making effectively New Zealand smoke-free by 2025;”. Treasury had such
trouble with that sentence that  it could not even express it properly. The syntax is all
skew-whiff. But, anyway, the first object ive, clearly, is about achieving the
Government’s fiscal strategy goals. If it were  not that, if it were seriously a health
measure—and I am pleased that Dr Hutchison is coming up to the Table to get a copy of
the bill so that he can prepare his arguments in rebuttal of this—it would say in Part 1 of
the bill, surely, would it not : “We are going to take th is money, which Treasury
calculates will be a substantial amount”—that  amount that my colleague quoted before,
and I am just struggling to find it—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: $528 million.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: It was $528 million over 4 years. It would say in Part 1,
if it were serious: “A proportion”—I am not going to be greedy and say all of the $528
million over 4 years, but a proportion; let us say a tenth—“would be dedicated to
assisting people to give up smoking.” A ssisting people to give up smoking—in other
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5711
words, putting money back into Quitline, putting money back into the products that
assist people who are addicted to nicotine to withdraw from  it, to manage it in the
course of that withdrawal, and to successfu lly give it up. That would be something to
really praise the Government about, had it been serious about this being a health
measure. But for all my examination of Part  1, I cannot find anythi ng that says that
these four substantive 10 percent increases are going to be put back into health. They
are not. They will be used to paper over the cracks of a disparate and an unsuccessful
economic strategy.
Although we support the bill, for health reasons—and I am sure that there will be one
or two well-intentioned members of the Gove rnment who support this bill for health
reasons—there are others who are simply saying: “Here is a tax grab. Here is something
that we can do, because we are falling terribly  short in our projec tions on what we are
going to get from asset sales. So we are not going to get the money that we expected to
get, the market is low, our assets are de preciating by the day, and we are not going to
get the funds that we  thought we would get from asset sales, and therefore we need
additional forms of revenue. What can we do ? We will hike up the cost of tobacco,
make cigarettes more expensive, and we can do it under the guise of it being good for
people.”
This is a cynical measure. However, havi ng spotted the cynicism, which one could
spot at 500 paces—at 500 paces—we are prepar ed to support the bill for all the right
reasons, and, in fact, recognise  that what should be in here is some mechanism for
delivering the revenue gathered from these f our 10 percent increases back into health
and health protection for New Zealanders.
There is more to be said about this. The bill is currently inadequate. It serves one
purpose and one purpose only, as a tax grab. If we are lucky, it will have a by-product
that will be good for New Zealanders, but it wa s not drafted with that in mind. If it had
been, it would have been drafted differently. Thank you.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: I am very happy to ta ke a short call on this
Committee stage of the Customs and Ex cise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures)
Amendment Bill, and I am saddened that the Opposition think that members of the
Government would be cynical ab out this in any way. This is a bill that is designed
purely and simply to improve the health of New Zealanders, by reducing smoking. This
Government is committed to reducing smoking harm in this country. This is about
increasing tobacco excise taxes by 10 percent, as  Part 1 of this bill outlines in detail.
The increases over the next 4 years, which a ltogether will add up to a very significant
additional burden, send a very clear message and a strong incentive to smokers in order
to encourage them to quit. In the meantime, the Government is providing in Budget
2012 $20 million over the next 4 years for the Pathway to Smoke-Free 2025 fund,
which helps fund programmes to discourage smoking and help smokers quit. I think that
what we are hearing from the other side is—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Claptrap.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: —claptrap. It is time that we focus on some of the details. So
I will be looking forward to some other speeches that focus more on the details of Part 1
coming forward. Thanks.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call and, in particular, to follow
up on the contribution from Paul Goldsmith, b ecause he did state—and he is the first
Government member to speak in this de bate—that the Customs and Excise (Tobacco
Products—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill is a bill intended to improve the health
of New Zealanders. That has been one of the topics that has been debated in this
Committee stage of the bill, and also in the second reading debate that we held earlier
this week.
5712 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
I think it is interesting, is it not, that ther e does seem to be general support from the
House for this bill. I think all parties will be voting for it—I am not sure about New
Zealand First, but all other parties will certainly be voting for it.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Have to wait and see.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: We will have to wait for someone to come back. But despite the
general support for the bill, none the less there are many suggestions about
improvements to the bill that have been ca nvassed both in the de bate and also by the
Finance and Expenditure Committee and by many of the submitters. It is an unusual
thing, it seems to me, that in the select committee’s report it refers to amendments to the
bill that it would have made had they been in  scope. I think that is an interesting point,
is it not, because it suggests that there are further public policy measures that we as a
nation ought to be taking around control of toba cco-related harm and that this bill does
not do the things that we need it to do. Iain  Lees-Galloway has mentioned that it is a
better approach than has been used to excise tax increases in the past, and I would agree
with that. I think it is a step forward. But, given the opportunity that the bill presented, it
is unfortunate that it did not go further.
I quote again from the letter to the New Zealand Medical Journal from Associate
Professor Nick Wilson and George Thomson from the Otago school of medicine from
earlier this week. They very clearly raised the question that  has been raised by several
speakers over the debate in this stage and earlier about what the purpose is of the bill. In
fact, what they said in their letter was: “W e suggest that Parliament makes it explicit in
the tobacco tax legislation that: the primar y purpose of the current Bill is to reduce
smoking so as to prevent harm to health and to prevent premature deaths, rather than to
increase Government revenue.” They also say that the purpose clause that they suggest
would say that “The Bill is a key part of the Government plans for achieving a
smokefree nation in 2025.” So that is placing into statute, in fact, that goal.
If, indeed, the linkage that Paul Go ldsmith has mentioned tonight is the
Government’s intention—that that is what this Government is a bout—then I invite the
Minister in the chair to bring a Supplementary  Order Paper to the floor of the House to
add exactly that kind of purpose clause. It has been drafted for the Government by the
professors at Otago medical school.
I think it is apparent, is it not, why that c onfusion has arisen. Those who believe that
the bill is, or ought to be, about reducing smoking-related harm would then look at the
options that were canvassed by the various agencies who were supporting the select
committee on this bill and note that the option th at was selected for inclusion in the bill,
and which is reflected in th e bill that has been reporte d back, was the option that
actually had the least positive impact on improving New Zealanders’ health. So either
there is some kind of goal confusion going on, and one suspects that that may be the
case—and if that is the case, then perhaps a purpose clause along the lines suggested by
those Otago professors would be helpfu l to everyone, to the public and to the
Government, and would be clear about what it was that it is trying to achieve—or else
there is something more insidious, and that is  certainly the theory that we have heard
espoused in the debate tonight. The Government is  able to settle that  point, if it was to
take up that suggestion about inserting a purpose clause.
The select committee rejected the more aggr essive measures that would have had a
more positive effect on health, and in doing so it also made some further comment in its
report to this House about, in fact, its doubt about whether the measures that were being
passed into law would be adequate to meet that 2025 goal. It suggested that there should
be some ongoing monitoring by the Government  of progress towards that goal, with a
view to determining whether further measur es are required. Again, the Minister in the
chair may or may not be in a position tonight to indicate what the monitoring regime is
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5713
that the Government intends to put in place to determine whether or not progress is
adequate towards that goal. Again, that would be a useful insertion into the bill by the
Government—the monitoring regime that it in tends to use to determine whether or not
these measures are achieving the goal. There is certainly a lot of doubt about that point.
It was raised by virtually every submitter to the select committee, and, certainly, all of
the experts. Indeed, the advice from the offi cials themselves suggests that the measures
in this bill will not be adequate to achieve th at purpose. I am certainly very keen to hear
from the Minister about what that monitoring regime will be.
I also want to touch on one other point in re lation to Part 1, and that is the matter of
duty-free tobacco concessions. This is the i ssue on which the select committee said that
had it been in scope it would have recommended an amendment to the bill to change the
duty-free concessions. I think what that sugge sts is that the recommendation that the
select committee does make, which is that the Government needs to consider this
matter—to consider the consistency of th e duty-free concessions with that smoke-free
Aotearoa goal—is clearly another point that we want to hear from the Minister on. What
is it that the Government is going to do to assess that consistency? What is the
legislative programme that we might expect to see to close that gap?
I think the evidence is pretty clear, as New Zealande rs move through airports or
otherwise access duty-free stores or duty-free supplies, that the availability of duty-free
tobacco and tobacco products is increasingl y an anachronism in an environment where
our strategy as a nation is to denormalise tobacco. Well, the massive stands of cigarettes
that we see in duty-free stores—I guess we do not see them now, but that we are used to
seeing—actually are the epitome of the normalisation of that product. This is a point
that does not, perhaps, affect very large numbers of people, but it is an important
symbolic step towards the goal that the Government has adopted of having a smoke-free
nation. I look forward to the comments from the Minister in the chair on exactly what it
is that the Government will do to close that gap.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: This Customs and
Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures ) Amendment Bill is a tax-grab. The
Government needs to be commended for sticking with this and coming this far.
Certainly, what is interesting is the re gulatory impact statemen t by Treasury. It is
quite fascinating. It says: “It does not assess and compare tobacco excise increases with
other revenue, savings and e xpenditure options Ministers ha ve considered in preparing
the 2012 Budget.” That clearly tells you that  they do not want to measure it, or
benchmark it, against anything. Two other pa rts are very interest ing: “Analysis to
inform a decision on tobacco excise increase s for Budget 2012 has included: the impact
of recent excise increases on Crown reve nue and on consumption patterns; likely
revenues from options to increase tobacco  excise; initial information on likely
distributional impacts … The analysis ha s not included”—has not included—“a range
of other issues due to time and resource constraints.”
I wonder how serious the Government is about this. It has no information here on the
“overall economic and fiscal impacts of smoki ng (eg: health and other welfare effects
on smokers, their families” and other impacts, and so on and so forth, and “disability
services linked to smoking … impact on the eco nomic welfare”, and so on and so forth.
We know full well that there are screeds a nd screeds and summaries of information on
the impacts of smoking. So the Government is just clearly trying to offset this, take the
money, and run—$528 million.
We heard the “Minister of Prisons” t oday going on about saving $170 million. I am
not too sure how you comprehend not expendi ng money on people’s welfare and trying
to avoid smoking, and going and building new prisons.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Rubbish!
5714 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: It is more than rubbish. It  is this new edict of the
right expecting that they can  take money off the working class and just do what they
like with it.
Tobacco in this country was a tool of th e colonisers—that is what it was—and it has
continued to be a tool of the colonisers, of  the Government. It seriously was—it was. I
say to this person over here, Andrew Williams, who was talking about the Asians, that it
is well known and scripted, if you are enough of an international scholar and understand
what happens to indigenous peoples, that wh en people in a settler society are being
oppressed or dominated by the majority, they do three things: they drink beer, they go
for sugar, and they smoke. That is the poor man’s correction, the working class’s
correction. The big-time colonisers grew bigger cigars, and they smoked cigars because
it was a pecking order thing. And I can assu re you that in a lot of these modern
countries that are coming into their own, th at is the first thing they do—they chase
sugar, they smoke, and they drink beer—beca use it is the poor man’s way to say that
they are going up in society. And we would be damned by a Government that does not
recognise that and wants to stop, you know, any brave movers.
I want to commend the great doctor over ther e, Dr Hutchison, because he stuck with
us when we knocked the smoking out of those restaurants and bars, when Simon
Bridges wanted to carry on smoking in restaurants in Tauranga.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Yes, you did. I remember you saying that. And
does it matter now? It is a great thing. So why do we not get serious about Part 1 and
ensure that it is knocked right out. We should be working towards that.
You know, Quitline and Auahi Kore cannot ev en pay their phone bills, and you are
going to flog the money off them—$528 milli on. Auahi Kore—there are a lot of
volunteers who run around in th ose cars. They tell me that it takes 4 weeks to
disconnect a heavy smoker and for them to even start to practise and be honest about
not smoking—4 weeks. It takes a lot of m oney. But you take it from me, sonny—that is
what happens.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Oh, sorry, Mr Chair. Kia ora, Mr Chair. Dear sir,
be assured that that is wh at people do when they come out from the boondocks: they
chase beer, they eat sugar, and they smoke cigarettes—and we s hould be aware of it.
There are more than enough M āori and Pasifika people who have respiratory diseases
and who have smoked themselves to death, and it will continue—it will continue. The
worst situation in relation to this bill is that there is not any money being put back in to
help correct it and to help support the correction. The doctor knows that. That is why he
is chewing on his glasses.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It is a delight to follow my
colleague the Hon Parekura Horomia, who has put his finger on a number of important
issues addressed in the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures)
Amendment Bill. He has really brought home some  of the issues that continue to affect
many members of our population, and he has drawn attention to  the need to have those
issues addressed more seriously than in the kind of haphazard way that the National
Party has sought to address them over the y ears—or not address them. I remind us all
that it is not so long ago that Bill Englis h himself opposed such a revenue increase by
the then Labour Government, saying that “the Government did not ever say it would do
it … that is the Government’s  standard, not ours.” He wa shed his hands of it. He
labelled it a tax increase and said that “It is a tax on the poorest people of New Zealand,
it is an increase that is far too large, and th at is why we voted against it.” So the finance
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5715
Minister, not so long ago, was voting against this kind of measure.  There is a certain
irony in his supporting it now.

items.speaker: We see it for what it is
items.text: it is a cynical tax grab—$528 million over the next 4 years,
Treasury says, will go into the Treasury coffe rs. We know that is why the Government
is doing it. We know it is concerned about the revenue hole left by the 4 percent revenue
drop during its term in office, which is la rgely due to economic conditions being poor.
This Government has the worst economic record  of any Government in 50 years. It had
hoped for better. It described its 2010 package as broadly fiscally neutral, and it has
proven to be anything but, unless one uses the term “broad” in the broadest sense.
We know that smoking remains the single biggest cause of preventable morbidity
and mortality in New Zealand. Around one in five adults currently smoke. The Customs
and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measur es) Amendment Bill di rectly affects a
significant portion of our populatio n. It is an issue that need s to be tackled. Labour will
be supporting the bill because this is a measure in the ri ght direction. We have had a
principled stance on this right the way through. It is not about a tax grab as far as we are
concerned; it is actually about addressing the health issue that lies behind it.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Holier than thou.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Labour continues to s upport this, we continue to be consistent
in this regard, and Maggie Ba rry will acknowledge that this is the right thing to do. I do
not think she would say it is the wrong th ing to do. Her Government is now supporting
this measure.
What we see is that, equally, in the papers that we have had before us in the Finance
and Expenditure Committee, the regulatory im pact statement from Treasury explains
the effect of this legislation on smokers. In 2010 Cabinet favoured the sequence of three
10 percent steps rather than a one-off 30 percen t increase, because it considered that it
would offer a repeated set of messages to smokers. That is what is contained in the
regulatory impact statement. It goes on to sa y that “The Treasury does not have any
evidence available to support one  approach over the other as  being more likely to be
effective in prompting sustained reductions in smoking.” I think that  what sits behind
this particular choice is that this Governme nt does not want to de al with it on multiple
occasions. It wants to get this dirty Act over with. It wants to get the revenue banked in
the coffers. It does not want to address the he alth issue too many times, so that is why it
has chosen the 30 percent over the 10 perc ent when it has had direct advice from
Treasury that it makes no difference whatsoever.
The effect on smokers, of course, is si gnificant. An average smoker smokes 12
cigarettes a day, we are told. Assuming a current price of $16 for a packet of 20, that
amounts to $3,500 per year. Contin uing to smoke those 12 ciga rettes per day, we are
told, will cost the average smoker an additional $1,130 more per year. This is a
significant measure. It will affect behaviour. It will make a difference because we know
that price and marketing is the most effec tive way of dealing with addictions. We know
that from the alcohol sphere. We see the Government avoiding t hose measures in the
alcohol sphere currently, but to its credit it is taking on the price issue here, albeit for
perhaps the wrong reasons.
Certainly the University of Otago presen ters who came to our select committee
identified that. They portrayed this bill, al though in more polite and academic terms, as
a naked revenue grab. They advocated for some changes in the bill. The first was to
clearly establish that the purpos e of the bill is to save li ves rather than to increase
Government revenue—to make the purpose abso lutely clear. Secondly, they advocated
for clearly establishing the bill as part of the Government’s plans for a smoke-free
nation in 2025. That is an interesting point th at I will come back to, because if it were
adopted as part of the Government’s plan for a smoke-free nation in 2025, we might see
5716 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
some additional measures, because Treasury al so tells us that this measure alone is
unlikely to achieve that goal. They also advocate for increasing the tax rises to 40
percent in the first instance, and at least 20 percent in subsequent rises.
The researchers from the University of Otago—whose specialist topic this is, who
have done the research, who understand what would make a change, and who are people
based and educated largely in New Zeala nd’s finest city—would recommend that we
also reduce duty-free allowances for tobacco products to one pack of 20 cigarettes or the
equivalent. They would also urgently i nvestigate establishing a minimum price for
tobacco. These are measures th at the select comm ittee did not decide to adopt. They
would further suggest that we ensure tax increases are implemented with co-
interventions, and they outline a series of ways in which that could be done, effectively
hypothecating the additional tax take. Perhaps it is a dirty word to Treasury—the “h”
bomb, hypothecation—but it is actually a wa y of having the changes accepted by the
public. We know that the public will accept po sitive changes, and particularly smokers
in the general public, when they know that th ey will be provided with assistance to help
break the habit as a part of that package. These researchers note that the overwhelming
evidence is that tax increases are one of  the most effective means to reduce smoking
prevalence. They cite the modelling work car ried out by the New Zealand Institute of
Economic Research for the Ministry of Health  that demonstrated that substantial tax
increases would be an important compone nt of achieving the 2025 smoke-free goal.
Treasury advises that the increas es proposed will not be suffic ient to achieve that goal
on their own.
We note that there is a paucity of other policy being brought forward by the
Government, and all of that, of  course, highlights the fact th at as far as the Government
is concerned this is an attempt to fill its revenue hole, the 4 per cent loss of revenue in
the Government books—1.5 percent of which is attributed by the Inland Revenue
Department to the global financial crisis, but 2.5 percent of which is attributed directly
to Government policy changes. This is an attempt to begin to fill that revenue hole
because the economy has not grown. The polic ies the Government has adopted, the tax
policies we are discussing here, and other policies the Government has adopted have not
grown the economy sufficiently that the revenu e is there to afford  the public services
that we all value. We see this  bill as a tax grab. Unfortuna tely, it is not achieving the
2025 goal that we would hope it would.
We also note that Treasury’s advice is th at the social policy objectives will not be
met, because excise increases should be considered as part of a broader package. They
also note that the stock of current smokers wi ll still be the majority of smokers in 2025.
Even aggressive increases in tobacco excise rates alone are unlikely to be sufficient to
achieve the smoke-free goal in this time frame. I put it to  you that this is clearly a
measure that is a tax grab. It is going to ac hieve positive results, so we will support it.
We do wish the Government would go further,  and I look forward to hearing from the
next member who will speak, and I hope it is Maggie Barry. I hope she will enlighten us
as to the wider Government po licy on this issue, and not just tell us about the naked tax
grab, which this current bill represents. Thank you.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I move, That the question be now
put.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Chair. I ri se knowing that that
botanical expert could visit upon me a form  of mother-in-law’s tongue, a well-known
weed that grows up in and ar ound the gardens of Auckland. Bu t I want to talk about a
far more serious subject.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Don’t be so prickly, Shane.
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5717

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: I was relying only on the modest botanical knowledge I
inherited from the Anglican Church while I wa s at St Stephen’s College. Then I went to
the various Anglican churches around Au ckland—and I must say the padre did smoke,
so it is actually relevant—and I recalled that line. I am not entirely sure whether that
member actually spoke about that botanical pe st otherwise known as the mother-in-
law’s tongue, but from time to time she evinces those qualities. That is reflective of how
much botanical knowledge she had, inversel y related to some of her political
contributions. Kei te pai.
I would like to start with a small story—very  instructive. I come  from the very far
north, Ninety Mile Beach, and the name of our tribe is Te Aup ōuri. It means the dense
smoke. How it arose was that we were surrounded by some of Hone Harawira’s
relations, and we were a far more modest, humble sort. In order for us to escape the
ravages of their foul designs, we lit a big fire. We waited for the smoke. It was early in
the morning and it settled just above the current of the water. We managed, with a level
of sleekness, and a sort of waka that was not a “Tupperwaka”, to sneak away.
Unfortunately, in more recent times, that  story—a grand story about pre-colonial
times—is visited upon us as more and more of my own matuas have died with a
cigarette, Park Drive, in the m āngai, one in the damn hands, and one in the ear. Those
images—unfortunately, they were M āori Battalion returnees, so  it is probably not the
most sensible contribution in  terms of the rather roman tic image we have about our
matuas who went to the Māori Battalion—were a feature.
When we went to hui, because I grew up right next to the marae—my dad was a
dairy farmer, which may cause some of the members on the other side of the Chamber
to ponder as to how I ended up where I am. Well , it was truth in just ice, it was truth in
justice—truth in justice. However, part of  what we contributed on the marae with our
old grandmother, who wh āngai-ed me, brought me up with my parents, etc.—she was
born in 1892—was that we used to go and ge t bales of hay and spread this hay out
because there were very few mattresses, etc. We would spread this hay out and put out a
thing called a kuta mat, made out of this gol den reed growing in th e lakes; our whaeas
used to make these mats out of it. So that was the mattress. Well, I have vivid memories
of these Māori Battalion returnees sitting there, with their Park Drive, with a small flask
of whisky, arguing about land.
Unfortunately, not much has changed, but at  least there has been an improvement.
The tone has changed and th e norms have changed. There is no more smoking in that
particular marae. We actually have mattre sses. I think they come from “The Ware-
whare”, otherwise known as The Warehouse. Unfortunately, fewer of us actually know
how to make those mats. They are one or  three long-suffering individuals who, from
time to time, have been mi sguided enough to support the M āori Party in the mistaken
belief that its politics are going to revive our culture, but that is another matter.
So this is just another step on a long-term journey. Yes, the tax is regressive and, yes,
I have been out once or thrice with my m ātāmua, the matua of Aotearoa Tuatahi, and,
yes, I have seen him with my partner enjoying a cigarette now and again. It is free will,
it is everyone’s choice, etc., and may th ey enjoy the opportuni ties that smoking and
drinking afford them. I enjoy drinking and so mething else but not smoking, but it is a
free life and it is free will. It is free will.
It is regressive, and a lot of our M āori voters, they are h ōhā. They are h ōhā that we
are supporting this, but we have to say to them: “It is in your best interests, and please
reward us appropriately when voting co mes around.” So we know that there are
occasional difficulties. I think it is inevitable th at the flinty, rather mean-spirited side of
the Chamber—that side of the Chamber—w ill remind us that this is about tax and
revenue, but it is how it is applied. I would actually like to see a hypothecation model—
5718 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
a rather sensible word brought to the fore by Annette King as she reformed our transport
policy, which is currently being squandered by that side of the Chamber. So this
revenue is dedicated to working with young parents. In our world, in Te Ao M āori,
unfortunately, a young parent of  16, 17, 18, or 19 in “Struggler s’ Gully” is often very
stressed, so the challenge that Treasury—
