items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Part 2 of the Customs
and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget M easures) Amendment Bill relates to
excluding price increases from required CPI indexation of, or related to, social
assistance. I was not on the select committee that considered this bill, being a member
of the Health Committee, not the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and I have to say
it is a pity that the chair of the Health Committee used  his call to take a closure motion,
rather than to offer a substantive contribu tion to the debate on Part 1. Maybe he will
offer more substance on Part 2.
What I understand the point of Part 2 to be is  to ensure that the excise tax increases
result in a significant real-term increase in  the cost of tobacco for the people who
receive income in any of the ways captured by Part 2 of this bill. The income that we
are talking about here concerns people who receive income that is related to the
Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act or to the Education Act 1989, with
that being student allowances; people who receive money through Working for
Families; people who receive money th rough New Zealand superannuation and
retirement income; people who receive social  security money; and people who receive
money through the War Pensions Act.
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5719
So what this aims to do is to ensure that the increase in the cost of tobacco is not
factored into any increases in those benefits or allowances and thus will not offset the
increase of the tobacco, so that in real terms the price of tobacco goes up. That is a
perfectly fine concept except for the fact, as Treasury points ou t, that one of the
unfortunate aspects of a tobacco tax increase is that it is regressive. It affects the people
on the lowest incomes the most and, indeed, it will certainly affect the people who
receive their income through any of these measures.
However, it will also affect people who receive their income through wages but who
are also on low income. However, people w ho receive their income through wages will
be able to argue that the increase in tobacco excise results in an increase in the
Consumers Price Index, and they will be able to bargain for a wage rise as a result. It
will certainly be factored into wage bargai ning around the country. So what you get, in
effect—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Two tiers.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: —is a two-tiered system. Exactly—thank you, Dr
Clark; you knew what I was going to say. It is a two-tier system whereby people who
receive an allowance or a benefit or a pens ion that is funded th rough taxes are going to
have their ability to offset this increase in the cost of living reduced, or, in fact, negated,
whereas those people who earn wages are not.
I guess it is similar, it is  analogous, in a way to the way the Government is behaving
around other people who receive a benefit. So, for instance, the Government has said
that women who receive a benefit will be able  to get free contraception. In fact, in an
interesting act of eugenics, their daughters w ill also be able to get free c ontraception.
But it is not all women on a low income, or, indeed, all women. It is singling out people
who receive a benefit. Likewise, parents who receive a benefit will now be required to
send their children to early childhood educa tion. It is not everybody. It is not making
early childhood education compulsory for ev erybody, but it is singling out for special
treatment people who receive a benefit, and this is anothe r instance of the Government
doing that. It is singling out people who receive a benefit, stigmatising the fact that they
receive a benefit by trea ting them differently from everybod y else. It is unfortunate that
this bill continues that theme that we have seen from this Government.
One thing that I find particularly interesting is the fact that this bill will pick on our
veterans who receive a pension by way of the War Pensions Act. Interestingly, the
Minister of Veterans’ Affairs is in the ch air at the moment, and he might have some
thoughts on this. This amendment to the War Pensions Act precedes much more
significant amendments to the War Pensions Act that veterans have been calling for, for
some years now. In fact, the Government has had a report in its ha nds for more than 2
years indicating how it could carry out the amendments to the War Pensions Act that are
required in order to make it more equitable and fair on those veterans who served before
1974, when ACC was introduced. Those are the types of amendments that veterans
want to see made to the War Pensions Act,  not this amendment, which will curtail any
increase that they might get to their pension to offset the increase in tobacco taxation—
the increase in cost for their cigarettes.
I understand what this part is about, what it is trying to achieve. It is trying to ensure
that these tax increases result in a real pr ice increase. I appreciate that, but, once again,
rather than ensuring that is the case for everybody, this Government is ensuring that it
particularly picks on the people who receive a benefit—not just the people who receive
an unemployment benefit or a sickness benefit or an invalids benefit but even the people
who receive New Zealand superannuation, and even the veterans who have served our
nation overseas, put themselves in harm’s way, and received injuries or illnesses as a
result of serving our nation over many decad es and in many conflicts around the world.
5720 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
This Government is going to pick on them by telling them it is going to make sure that
their pension cannot be increased as a result of the Consumers Price Index indexing that
would be linked to this bill. It comes as  no surprise—no surprise—that once again this
Government picks on anybody who r eceives their income in that  way. It is stigmatising
them and singling them out in the way that this Government knows how.
Although we understand the point behind th is part, we have to point out the
inadequacy of the way the Government has done it, and the fact that, once again, people
who receive a benefit or Government assist ance are being singled out by this National-
led Government.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: I want to start by labelling this
part of the Customs and Excise (Tob acco Products—Budget Measures) Amendment

items.speaker: Bill as what it is
items.text: it is a cyni cal political move. It is a very , very cynical political move.
Part 2 of the bill is shameful. Government  members should be embarrassed by this. We
know they are embarrassed, because they have not taken any calls. We have not heard a
word out of the Minister in the chair all ev ening. We have not heard a word about this
part of the bill. We saw no one attempt to get up to speak to it from the Government
benches. They know that this is simply cynical politics and that it is difficult to defend.
How do we know that it is cynical politic s? Well, we need look no further than the
regulatory impact statement, which was publis hed in April 2012 in order for Ministers
to consider this legislation. In April 2012 the advice was wr itten, and the policy that the
Cabinet considered appears to have no men tion—no mention at all, as far as we can
see—in the regulatory impact statement of  this measure to target those who are
dependent on welfare to feed their familie s and to go about their daily business. We
know that this has been added on subsequently . It has been put in place to make sure
that an extra kick is put in to distract from the wider impact of this bill.
This is not atypical of the Government. We know that this is a pattern. We have seen
it happening. We know that whenever bad news comes around, there is more drug
testing for beneficiaries, there is compulso ry early childhood education, and there is a
range of other measures, which the Government has subsequently admitted it cannot
actually put into place but it  uses as a distraction. Here , again, we have a targeting
measure for beneficiaries, one that makes sure they will suffer the most. They will
suffer the most. All of those who are smokers will suffer as a result of this legislation.
All of them will face increased prices. But th is Government is determined to make sure
that those who are on hard times are kicked  while they are down, because it believes
that that is what is necessary in order to change the world.
Well, we disagree. We on this side of the Chamber have a more optimistic view of
human nature. We think people actually want jo bs, and if this Government had not lost
so many jobs, if it was not  sending 50,000 New Zealanders a year to Australia, then,
actually, people would have j obs and they would not be affected by this Draconian
measure, which will make it much harder for those on benefits than for anybody else to
afford the substantial increases in tobacco prices that are proposed in this bill.
Treasury, in its regulatory impact statemen t, recommends the revenue grab of $528
million, which the Government conveniently wants to adopt because it is well aware
that there is a hole in  the books as a result of the wo rst economic record in 50 years,
which this Government has perpetrated. The re gulatory impact statement says that “The
Treasury favours a sequence of regular modest , and well-signalled increases in tobacco
excise. This is likely to contribute most to a long-term and sustainable strategy to reduce
smoking rates.” There is a little bit of inconsis tency with an earlier part of the advice,
but for the greater part this is good Treas ury advice. The regulat ory impact statement
does say that “In taxing a group of consumers that are addicted a nd disproportionately
drawn from Maori and lower-socio econom ic communities, the Government should
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5721
ensure that programmes to educate and su pport smokers to make successful quit
attempts are adequately resourced, well implemented, and effectively designed and
targeted to reach high-risk groups.”
That is not what we see here in this bill. We do not see anything here going towards
meeting the needs of those most affected. In this bill, which is cynically targeted at
those who are struggling the most, we do not  see any additional measures signalled—
none whatsoever—to make sure that those group s that are targeted are given assistance
to give up smoking, which we a ll know and accept is so harmful. So that is why I say
that this is a cynical political move. We have  seen so much of it from this Government.
It is very good at sideshows and distractions , because it is very nervous. It is very
nervous about what the polls are showing. The polls are showing that its poor economic
record, the scandals around the Dotcom affa ir, the scandals in the ACC system, the
inability to tackle the big issues, and the focus on tinkering are doing it no good—doing
the Government no good whatsoever. That is why it is coming back  to these cynical
strategies, which target and kick those who are down.
The Treasury advice was to put additional measures to support those—

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Malo ni, Mr Chair. To use a word that David
Clark used, Part 2 is a cynical  and poor attempt by the Govern ment to make it look like
it is trying to do something for the public good in this bill, the Customs and Excise
(Tobacco Products—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill, to stop New Zealanders
smoking. It is a poor and cynical attempt at trying to make the Government look like it
is trying to do something to cut down smoking within New Zealand.
It was an honour and a privilege to sit in the 49 th Parliament on the Health
Committee, chaired by Dr Paul Hutchis on—I look around me and I see Iain Lees-
Galloway, who was on that committee, and Kevin Hague, who was on that committee—
and to take some real action against tobacco companies and actually remove tobacco
displays from our shops. As you see, if you go  to a service station or a dairy today, you
will notice that there are no longer any displays  for tobacco or for ci garettes. It was an
absolute pleasure to be on that committee as  we worked across this Parliament—apart
from the exception of maybe a couple of ACT MPs who voted against that legislation—
to take some real action to reduce the numb er of Kiwis starting to smoke and to make
sure we get as many Kiwis quitting smoking as we possibly could.
But this bill, and especially Part 2 of it, is not motivated by trying to reduce the
number of smokers or to stop people star ting smoking. As a number of my colleagues
have said, this is simply a cash grab. It was sa id that this Government is trying to get its
mitts on $528 million over the next 4 years because of its failed economic policies, and
the fact that it could not and has not ra ised enough money to come through with its
policies. So that is what this part, Part 2, and what this bill is really about. Is it
motivated by cash revenue, by trying to raise revenue, or is it motivated by trying to
reduce the harm that smoking causes in our communities?
I want to take a quick l ook at the Pacific smoking numbers. As Iain Lees-Galloway
said in Part 1 of the deba te, just below one in five New Zealanders are smoking, and
unfortunately for the Pacific community it is over-represented in the smoking statistics,
because 27 percent of Pacific adults are sm okers. Unfortunately for Pacific men, that
number is 34.5 percent, so one-third of P acific men smoke, and one in five—just over
20 percent—of Pacific women smoke. In term s of the revenue that is going to be
gathered from this bill, it is surely the Pacific community by its over-representation in
the numbers of smokers that is going to be  over-represented in  this. Every year 100
Pacific people die because of heart diseas e come about because of smoking in that
community, 30 die of lung cancer because of  their smoking, and 23 Pacific people die
from strokes because of the fact that they have been smoking. So smoking does have a
5722 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
disproportionate effect on the Pacific community, and that is  why we want this bill to
actually take some strong measures, motiv ated by public good—public health good—to
make sure it takes some swift action and deci sive action to make su re, at least from the
Pacific perspective, that those numbers could be reduced.
We could actually use some of the $528 milli on that is going to come via this bill by
increasing the excise tax by 10 percent in those 4 years, and hypothecate it to make sure
it is going into smoking cessation progra mmes and into preventing young Pacific
Islanders taking up smoking. Those statistics th at I pointed out before are just awful.
Being a Tokelauan, it is the worst of all Pacific nations in terms of smoking, because 42
percent of the Tokelauan population are smoke rs. So as someone from that community,
I think we really need to make sure we are targeting our Pacific people—a large and
growing population in New Zealand—to make su re we are doing as much as we can to
use some of this money that we are raising to target them to say “Don’t start smoking.”,
or to take steps to reduce or stop smoking. I do not think that this bi ll is motivated by
trying to decrease those numbers.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to have a short
call on this Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures) Amendment
Bill. I would think that every perceptive member of Parliament would be celebrating the
quick passage of this bill, Parts 1 and 2, rather than being cynical about it.
I want to talk just on Part 2 for a mo ment. If one looks at the general policy
statement, it says this: “Continuing these excl usions ensures that recipients of social
assistance are not reimbursed for the increa ses in tobacco duties. Any reimbursement
for those increases would contradict the reason for making them, which is to discourage
smoking.” And we all know that an excise tax is probably the most effective measure in
diminishing smoking in this country.
But I want to say a little bit more. This bill  is just another step forward in many steps
towards achieving a smoke-free New Zealand, and under National there have been some
very significant steps. Firstly, there is the fact that we have made diminishing smoking
one of the very successful health targets. Th is has had a huge impact over the last 2 to 3
years. Secondly, we have put more money into Quitline funding and counselling.
Thirdly, as I speak, tobacco displays are disappearing thr oughout the shops and
supermarkets of New Zealand. And fourthly, of  course, we have backed that up with 4
years—one year after another—of 10 percent increases in the excise tax, which will be a
hugely significant step towards diminishing smoking in this country.
This bill is not to be viewed cynically; it is  to be celebrated as a great public health
measure.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: Part 2 of this Customs and Excise (Tobacco
Products—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill is what is currently under debate at the
moment in this Chamber and I need to raise some questions about Part 2 because my
colleagues have raised some significant points in  previous contributions, but I am not
sure that everybody watching this debate understands what the significance of Part 2 is.
Part 2 of this bill excludes the price increases on tobacco—these ones that happen,
the 10 percent increase, on 1 January every year  for the next 4 years. It excludes that
price increase from the basket of goods th at are considered wh en calculating the
Consumers Price Index. When calculating how much the cost of everything has gone up
this year, and therefore what the Consumers Price Index should be in order to bring up
people who are on benefits, whose benefits  are CPI indexed, pe ople go out and they
work out what people spend their money on. What do people spend most of their money
on? Well, they might spend most of their money on food, they might spend some money
on petrol, they might spend some money on childcare, they might spend some money
on clothing, they might spe nd some money on alcohol, an d they might spend some
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5723
money on tobacco. And so in this legislation the basket of goods, whether it is fruit and
vegetables, chicken or meat, or  all those other things that are put together in order to
calculate what the C onsumers Price Index should be, will  leave out the expenditure on
tobacco. And who for? For people who ar e receiving payments under the Children,
Young Persons, and Their Families Act—payments to the people or organisations that
are providing care for children—so that is th e caregivers. It will take out anybody who
is on a student allowance. It will take out  anybody who is getting Working for Families
entitlements. It will take out anybody getti ng New Zealand superannuation. It will take
out anybody who is receiving any of the main so cial security benefits . It will take out
anybody in long-term residential care, and it will take out people whose income comes
from veterans pensions.
So the point of this, if I understand it corre ctly—I am just looking in the direction of
the officials for a moment—is that the CPI ba sket of goods that is assessed on what
most people spend their money on, and how much  that has gone up compared with last
year, will exclude tobacco for people on benefits, those benefits I have outlined and
those other payments and entitlements I have  just described. In other words, if you
spend a lot of money on tobacc o, or if people generally spend a proportion of their
income on tobacco, that will not be taken into account for the purposes of calculating
the CPI and thereby raising people’s benefits.
This is a device. It is something that coul d be excused, that coul d even be justified,
but my question to the Government is, where is the consistency? Where is the
consistency? If tobacco is bad for people a nd this is a health measure, then why not
exclude it from the CPI indexa tion across everything, not just  the benefits that people
are going to have to live on in order to survive?
The CPI is important for wage negotiations . Unions go into wage negotiations on
behalf of their members, wa nting to compensate for the Consumers Price Index and the
increase in prices that have happened in the previous year, because unions do not want
their members’ incomes—wages and salary —to fall behind prices. Therefore, the
Consumers Price Index is important. It is impor tant to wage and sala ry earners, as well.
So why is this tobacco provision being applie d to beneficiaries only? I ask the Minister
in the chair, Anne Tolley, if it is a good thing to do, then is  it not a good thing to do for
everybody? If this is a health measure, would it not benefit everybody’s health?
I can understand the import of  excluding it from the CPI calculation, but what I
cannot understand is simply targeting benefits  in that respect. That, to me, does not
make sense. If any member opposite says that  I am wrong about this, that I have got the
wrong end of the stick, would they please get up and take a call because it needs
explaining. I ask whether the Minister who move d this bill, Tariana Turia, could get up
and make some explanation as  to why only benefi ciaries are going to have this item
excluded from the basket of things that go into a CPI calculation—in other words, their
benefit will go up by the CP I, but not by as much as it w ould if it were taking tobacco
into account.
So I can see that the Government saves mone y in the process, but why is this being
applied only to beneficiaries? This is the ki nd of discrimination that I thought we were
not tolerating in this country, but now perh aps that the gap between the rich and the
poor in New Zealand has become so pronoun ced, and the people on benefits are so
much at the bottom of the heap these days, the Government has decided that it does not
really matter how they are treat ed any longer. All we hear ab out is social obligation; all
we hear is what people ought to be doing fo r themselves. When their lives hit some
rough patches the Government’s expectation is that they will pull themselves up by their
own bootstraps and correct their own circumstances, which is not always possible.
5724 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
However, the Government is blind to that  kind of consideration and simply makes
this exclusion of the price increases from the required CPI indexation related to social
assistance. In fact, those are the words on the page, “related to, social assistance”. If a
member opposite can contradict that for me, please get up and tell me I have got it
wrong, but that is what I read on the page . I see all the members opposite studiously
looking down and busy doing work so that they  do not have to look  as if they are
responding or listening. I would like somebody, a Minister, any Minister—

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: Are you voting for or are you voting against it?

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: —Mrs Collins—any Minister, not just the Minister in
the chair although I would welcome her particip ation, but also the Minister interjecting,
I would welcome her clarification around this , as well. It seems to me that it is
discriminatory. It is not fair. It is bashing the people at the bottom of the heap again, and
somehow this Government is going to turn it into a health measure. When you are at the
bottom of the heap and you are struggling to survive on care payments or benefits, then,
quite frankly, the health inequalities that descend upon you are insurmountable and they
become almost the last thing you are able to contend with as you are busy trying to
make ends meet.
I would welcome the intervention of any Nation al member here to correct me in this
respect. If I am not wrong, then this is discri minatory. This is not reasonable, and it is
simply another example of this bill being a tax grab and not a he alth measure. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: I just want to follow
on, as I said in Part 1, from that great speech  from Maryan Street by saying that this
measure is more than cynical, it is one of the most outrageous alignments of officials
under Ministers’ directions in not recognising th at. I want to go with what I read out in
debate on Part 1 in relation to this: “The analysis has not included a range of other
issues due to time and resource constraint s. Key gaps in the information include—
overall economic and fiscal impacts on sm oking (eg: health …”, and it goes down to
“the fiscal costs of publicly funded health a nd disability services linked to smoking; or
fiscal offsets such as reduced superannuati on and aged-care expend itures due to the
lower life expectancy of smokers)—impact  on the economic welfare of smokers and
their families;”.
As Maryan Street says and suggested, this is an incredible situation where
beneficiaries are being more than bullied, they are being separa ted out. Why do we not
do the same thing to the lawyers and accountants in this country? They all have lips and
lungs that suck in the smoke. Why is it so  different that it should be left to
beneficiaries? In the sense of the redi stribution, if you are going to hold $528 million,
and the $170 million that the Minister in the chair, Anne Tolley, said in a speech today
that she saved from building the big prison, where the hang are we going? That is nearly
$700 million. Where is that going to? Is it going to fill up the potholes on the way to the
golden mile above Auckland? Is it going to do other things? I join with Maryan Street
and say that this is callous—

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: That’s not a picture I would like to see, Pare.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: No, no, there are people in Rotorua who smoke
and people down in Clendon who smoke. There are a lot of people there who are
beneficiaries, and you have not done too well as—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Those people there have not done very well. When
you are running at an unemployme nt rate of 15 percent for M āori and Pasifika people,
and 74 percent of them are smokers, where do you get the relief or the recognition in
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5725
relation to ensuring that the tax grab is at  least redistributed amongst some of those
people?

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: Are you for it or against it? Which one? I’m just checking.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: That member over there can chortle and laugh and
chatter and clatter, but at the end of the day this is outrageous. This is terrible.
I want just one of them, including the Minister, to take a call and tell me why—as Dr
Hutchison will always suggest—beneficiaries  and superannuitants are sorted out in
isolation. Why not the other people? Why not  the lawyers and accountants in Parnell?
Why not the ones who live around Massey Univ ersity, all those academics? Why not
them? Why just the beneficiaries? Their life is so tortured anyway that they jump on the
plane and they go to Australia. You just slip this through.
I want to mihi to the officials. They are hard-working people, but they are clearly
under the Minister’s directions, because that is  the same Minister who said that he did
not support this—“W īremu P ākehā”. That is what he sa id. He did not support the
smoking issue when we were trying to put it  through. I want to th ank the past Labour
Government for ensuring that all those people who puffed smoke around you in
restaurants and bars had to comply, and we were bold and game enough to do it to
everybody, not just the benefici aries. We made sure that  everybody who went in there
had to comply, and it was recognised that  this was everybody—as the great preacher
says, all the sinners. So let us not deny it and say that some are and some are not. That is
what is happening in this Part 2.
It is outrageous. Poor old beneficiarie s, poor old solo mums, and poor old
superannuitants. And then there is this callous statement that  there could be some fiscal
adjustments because of lower life expect ancy. What the hang do you think, if you let
people carry on smoking? You cannot have Qu itline when you run around the country
saying: “Yeah, we’ve got broadband in.”, but it cannot even pay for its phone bill. That
is the free 0800 number that these people have. So I think Part 2 of this bill is one of the
most—

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Dastardly.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chairperson. Ka pai.
It is an honour again to follow the Hon Pa rekura Horomia. I have certainly drawn the
long straw tonight in getting to follow his fabulous speeches, which get to the nub of the
matter and the discrimination that is being put forward in this particular part of the bill,
the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products —Budget Measures) Amendment Bill. Of
course, we should not lose sight  of the fact that this is actually a step in the right
direction, in terms of the overall bill. But th is part, for those who are listening at home,
is a part of the bill that is aimed at targe ting beneficiaries and maki ng sure that life is
tougher for them than for anybody else.
The overall bill, of course, attempts to make sure that the increases in tobacco pricing
reduce the incidence of tobacco -related harm, and that is th e good part of the bill. We
know that National opposed such measures when it was in Opposition, so we are a little
bit suspicious, of course, of the timing, now that it has a great big fat revenue hole that it
is trying to fill. We have heard no word at all from the Minister in the chair through the
whole debate, and we are beginning to w onder whether there is no response to the
accusation that this is a revenue grab. It seems to be pretty jolly clear that it is, and I
guess the Government is too embarrassed to ev en try to argue otherwise, and that is
consistent with what this Government is doing.
We have heard about the tax on paper boys, the tax on cleaners in schools, and so on,
which are the moves the Government has taken in  order to make sure that it is grabbing
5726 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012
taxes wherever it can, because it does not have a plan for the economy. The
Government does not have pro-growth tax pol icy proposals. It is not proposing to put
taxes in place that would support manuf acturing industries and would support our
exporters. Instead, the Government is dete rmined to get tax where it can off the
vulnerable and to run down our public serv ices through a reduced tax take and ever-
reducing budgets. We know that the Govern ment has the worst economic record in 50
years, and so it is no surprise in some ways that this tinkering bill is a little bit cynical
and nasty at points.
We know, also, and this is in some advice that we re ceived in the Finance and
Expenditure Committee, that the tobacco industry, of course, will find ways to mitigate
the impact of tobacco tax increases. It will smooth the transition to higher prices,
introduce lower price brands, and so on. It is documented behaviour that the researchers
put in front of us in the select committ ee hearings. Unfortunately, those on the very
lowest incomes, those who are beneficiaries, wh om this part of the bill targets, will not
have the luxury of riding out price increases  in the same way. We know it is likely that
some families will suffer. When we live in a situation where a large portion—25
percent—of the children in this country are living in poverty, it is disastrous that no
commensurate measures are put in place to address this issue in the beneficiary
population. The fact is that th e budget will be tighter agai n for them, but no additional
measures are put in place to ensure that they have the tools and support necessary to
kick this damaging habit.
I want to put on record again that the Labour Party does support this bill overall
because it is important that we reduce tobacco- related harm. We are glad that the scales
have fallen from the Government’s eyes. It is a shame that it took a great big revenue
hole to make that happen, but the scales fell from its eyes in order to see the need to
increase the excise on tobacco, thereby reducin g over time, as the research tells us, the
incidence of tobacco-related harm. We know that where there are support measures in
place, the public and those affected by this kind of legislation will support it. We know
that the Government is choosing in Part 2 to put an additional burden on those who are
struggling the most, but choosing not, at the same time, to put additional support
measures in place. That is why this part of the bill is an embarrassment. We know it was
a late political fix, a late political addi tion, because it is not spoken about in the
regulatory impact statement that was consider ed by Cabinet. It is not considered in
there. It is a cynical move to target the most vulnerable.
I would really like to hear some attempt at justification from the Minister in the
chair. We have heard nothing all evening fr om the Minister in the chair about this
measure. We have heard very little from the Minister in the chair indeed—

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: The title of this bill is
the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Produc ts—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill.
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5727
Actually, often what the Opposition does in these debates is we offer alternative titles to
the bill—what it might more appropriately be named. But in this case I think this is an
appropriate title. In fact, the title reveals wh at the actual intentions  of the Government
are in this bill, because spec ifically it is about excise, tobacco products, and Budget
measures. It is a Budget measure. The Budget measure, of course, that this bill relates to
is trying to find ways to fill the hole left in the Government’s revenue sources, both
through its inadequate work on the economy and through its unaffordable income tax
cuts that it made, which it told the nation we re going to be fiscally  neutral, but have
actually left a huge hole in the Government ’s revenue. As the debate has gone on
tonight we have come to understand the real  significance of this le gislation, because it
does two things—in Part 1 and Part 2.
The first part is a massive increase in revenue for the Government, to make up for
some of that lost revenue, with no hypot hecation into any smoking cessation measures
or any treatment of diseases that are related to smoking. Part 2, of course, limits the
Government’s liability for paying out benefits , not just the sickness benefit and invalids
benefit but also pensions, also payments to people who are caregivers, and also to
people who receive a veterans pension. So, actually, as much as we, on this side of the
House, are really pleased to see the G overnment doing something—we know one of the
results of this bill will be to have an impact on the number of people who are smoking
and the amount that they smoke—the more an d more that we analyse this piece of
legislation, the more it is revealed that this  has got more to do with trying to increase
revenue for the Government, and limit its costs, than it has with anything to do with
health.
Let us look at the facts. It was not introduced by the Minister of Health. It did not go
to the Health Committee. In fact, if it had gone to the Health Committee, perhaps some
more of the changes that would be useful in this bill would have been recommended,
because it would have been viewed through the lens of a health initiative, rather than a
financial initiative, and rather than a tax b ill, which is simply about increasing revenue
and limiting liabilities and costs for the Government. So, indeed the title of this bill and,
in fact, the purpose of this bill, as well, are absolutely accurate— they are absolutely
accurate—because the bill makes no mention of  health measures, it makes no mention
of trying to reduce the incidence of smoki ng, it makes no mention of  trying to ensure
that fewer people die of tobacco-related di seases every year, it makes no mention of
improved funding for tobacco health initiatives—it makes no mention of any of that. All
this bill does is increase revenue and reduce costs.
Also, if this was a health initiative and the Government was focused on ensuring that
everybody, every smoker, was going to be properly impacted on by this legislation, then
we would not see the deliberate targeting of people who receive a benefit in the way that
we see in Part 2 of this legislation. The G overnment had an option. It had the option to
remove the tobacco excise increase from the CPI calculation for everybody, but it did
not do that. It could have, but  it did not. It chose instead to deliberately pick on people
who get some form of Government assist ance, whether it be through Working for
Families, whether it be through a ve terans pension, whether it be through
superannuation, or whether it be because that  person is a caregiver . For a whole host of
reasons, if that money came fr om the Government, then th at is the person that the
Government has chosen to pick on. It did not need to do that—it did not need to do
that—and that is what this bill is all about.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Mr Chair, I hope you will excuse
me. I am working under a pseudonym. I rise to speak to the—perhaps appropriately
addressed—title debate. I want to go a step  further than my colleague Iain Lees-
Galloway, although I support the se ntiment entirely in his addr ess on this topic. He
suggests that the bill, the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget Measures)
Amendment Bill, is perfectly named because it does not mention the health benefits. It
is a tax bill so, therefore, we might well view it as an appropriately labelled bill.
I think I would want to go one  step further to make a lit tle more explicit what the
purpose of this bill is. I would like to  see it renamed. I guess we will ask the
Government to consider this suggestion and, you know, present its argument as to
whether it is a useful one or not. My suggestion is that  we rename it the “Fill the
Revenue Hole but Decrease Smoking as an Unintended Consequence Bill’, because I
believe that that is what the bill actually does—that is what the bill actually achieves.
The reason why the bill is an unintended consequence is that the facts line up and say
that increases in revenue actually do di scourage smoking, and we  know that smoking
remains the single biggest cause of prev entable morbidity and mortality in New
Zealand. There is good reason to address this problem, esp ecially when half of all long-
term smokers die as a result of  smoking-related illness. That is about 5,000 deaths each
year that are attributable to smoking either directly or through an indirect route like
second-hand smoke. But unlike National when it was in Opposition, Labour has
supported Government moves to reduce sm oking in New Zealand. Labour has been
consistent in supporting moves to reduce sm oking in New Zealand, an d that is why we
see, if we look back, that this title hi ghlights, I guess, the irony in the National
Government moving this bill. It says that the decreasing of smoking is an unintended
consequence, and that it really is about the revenue-grabbing.
How do we know that? We know that because when in Opposition, Bill English, who
is now obviously concerned about the revenue hole that this Government is facing, said
that it was a tax increase when Labour  moved measures. When Labour moved
extraordinary urgency to increase the excise on tobacco in the early 2000s, Bill English
said “It is a tax on the poorest people in New Zealand. It is an increase that is far too
large.” So he labelled it a tax increase. That  is what he thought it was, nothing more,
nothing less—nothing more, nothing less. So th at is why we know that it is an
unintended consequence that it is actual ly addressing smoking, a nd why the title “Fill
the Revenue Hole but Decrease Smoking as an Unintended Conseque nce Bill” is a far
more fitting title than the one that the Government has proposed.
So I move that we consider that title. I do not formally move it. I move it in the sense
of having a debate about it and inviting the Government to consider that as a more
fitting title, a more honest title, and as a title  that would reflect the content of the bill,
which is presumably what a title is designed to achieve, so that we could have a bill that
reflects the Government’s real intention, whic h is about filling this revenue hole, which
it has no other plans or means to do so.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: It does concern us what has been dropped on us here in
terms of this bill in relation to beneficiarie s, superannuitants, and those in the country.
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5729
This is a pretty miserable, late-minute thing that the Government is doing here, in terms
of just sliding something through that is, again, an attack on beneficiaries and those who
are in need of support from the State.
The reason I was a bit slow getting to my  feet was that I was just doing some
calculations on this in terms of the CPI, a nd was looking at the effects of the CPI on
superannuitants and on beneficiaries. Wh en you are looking at a single-income
beneficiary on about $400 a week, or a couple on a bit over $600 a week, and if you are
looking at the difference in the CPI effect b ecause of taking tobacco out of the CPI or
keeping it in, it is such a small amount of  money from the point of view of the
Government’s revenue, but it can actually have an impact on the beneficiaries. Although
to us it might not appear a lot of money, every few dollars every week adds up. I think it
is really very much a situation of penny-pi nching again, on the part of the Government,
that a few dollars out of every beneficiar y’s pockets could be affected through the
adjustment in the CPI by not including tobacco in the CPI.
It really is back to the “F agin Budget” that I have mentioned in Parliament on a few
previous occasions. The Government has al ready taken money off the paper boys and
the paper girls—taken $14 million off them. Having taken $14 million off the children
of this country, now it is goi ng to adjust the CPI so that the CPI also reflects that
tobacco is not included in the CPI. It is really getting down to real miserable penny-
pinching - type budgetary constr aints. In that regard, it is  creating a situation in New
Zealand where you have a CPI for some and you have a CPI for others, and where the
CPI applies to those with money on a higher level of CPI, and those who are on welfare
support have a different CPI adjustment.
In particular, in regard to the senior citizens in this country and those on
superannuation—many of whom are not smokers; many of whom have not smoked—
why should they be penalised and have some sort of alteration to the CPI adjustment
and an increase, simply because this Govern ment wants to be miserable and claw back
some money because of the 10 percent annual increase each year for the next 4 years on
cigarettes? You know, it really is starting to bite close to the bone in terms of our senior
citizens, in particular, and those with disabilities and t hose on welfare who through no
fault of their own and in times of difficult y, due to ill health or disability, or because
they are aged, are requiring support from the State.
New Zealand First will not be supporting th is part of the bill. We do support the
overall thrust of the bill in terms of the health aspects and reducing cigarette smoking
and tobacco consumption, but when it gets down to starting to penny-pinch to attack
those who are the most vulnerable in New Zealand society—
Denis O’Rourke: And the elderly.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: —and, in particular, the elderly, who would be affected by
a reduced adjustment on their superannuation increases from the CPI being cut back in
terms of beneficiaries—then I am sorry but th is is another case of the Tory Government
being very miserable to people who deserve better. So New Zealand First will not be
supporting this part of the bill.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak
to Supplementary Order Paper 129, moved on behalf of the Hon Tariana Turia. What
this Supplementary Order Paper does is that it divides the Customs and Excise (Tobacco
Products—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill into a number of bills. This will separate
out all those separate pieces of legislation that need to be amended in order to
discriminate against different people who receive income from the Government.
The Labour Party will be voting in favour of this Supplementary Order Paper to
separate the legislation, but I would like to indicate at this  point that it will be our
intention, when it comes time to  vote on those separate pie ces of legislation, to vote
against the individual bills that  will relate to that specifi c measure that the Government
is taking. We will vote in favour of the new Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—
Budget Measures) Amendment Bill, but we  will vote against the Children, Young
Persons, and Their Families (Indexation—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill, the
Education (Student Allowances Indexation—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill, the
Income Tax (Working for Families Indexation—Budget Measures) Amendment Bill,
the New Zealand Superannuation and Re tirement Income (Indexation—Budget
Measures) Amendment Bill, the Social Security (Indexation—Budget Measures)
Amendment Bill, and the War Pensions (Indexation—Budget Measures) Amendment
Bill, because we believe that the Government has taken completely the wrong approach
in discriminating against a certain set of New Zealanders who will not have the ability
to be reimbursed, I suppose, for this increase, whilst allowing others to be able to do so.
We understand what the Government is trying  to achieve in increasing the cost of
tobacco in real terms and ensuring that there are fewer opportunities to offset that.
However, if the Government’s true intention was for that impact to be spread fairly
across all smokers, then it would have taken an approach whereby the CPI calculation
for all smokers would not include the tobacco  tax increase. Rather, it has taken the
approach that only those who receive some fo rm of income from the Government will
be affected. That is why the Labour Party is  certainly happy to se e the separation of
these bills, because we want to be able to vo te for the parts of this bill that we think
make sense.
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5731
We agree that increasing tobacco taxation is one way of reducing the harm caused by
tobacco. We suspect that the Government’s real motivation behind doing that is to make
up for its lost revenue, but we do appreciate the perhaps unintended consequence for the
Government of doing so—that it will reduce to bacco-related harm. So we want to be
able to vote for that aspect of the bill, bu t we actually appreciat e that this amendment
will allow us to vote against those measures that we think are rather insidious and create
just one more division between people who receive income from the Government and
other New Zealanders. That is certainly what this Government’s approach has been over
the last few weeks: to drive that wedge be tween some New Zealanders and others as
hard as it can. It wants to see people fighting amongst themselves. It wants to see people
pointing the finger of blame at the victims of  poverty rather than trying to do something
about it. This bill, in its own small way, has been found out t onight as being part of that
Government programme to continue to discriminate against anybody—anybody. It is a
broad brush in this bill; even the poor vetera ns are getting hit with this bill. So we
certainly support—
Denis O’Rourke: Superannuitants.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: And the superannuitants—you are absolutely right. The
superannuitants, the families who receive Working for Families—a whole range of
people are going to be unnecessari ly discriminated against with  this legislation. So it is
good that this bill will be separated out into  its component parts by this Supplementary
Order Paper in the name of the Hon Tarian a Turia. That will give the right-minded
parties in this Chamber the oppor tunity to vote for those asp ects of the legislation that
will do good, and against those aspects of the legislation that will do harm.
It is a noble idea to ensure that the excise tax increase results in an increase in real
terms in the cost of tobacco, but it is not noble at all—it is as far from noble as is
humanly possible to be—to determine that one  group of New Zealanders will be hit by
that methodology and others will escape from it.
The Labour Opposition is very happy to s upport this Supplementary Order Paper in
the name of the Hon Tariana Turia. We think it will be useful—it will be quite useful—
because it actually will allow Parliament to reveal what so me of these measures really
are, what their true intended purpose is, and will give Opposition parties the opportunity
to cast their votes accordingly. As I have said, I want to signal that tomorrow during the
third reading debate on these bills, as th ey will be by then, the Labour Opposition will
certainly be voting against those measures th at discriminate against people who receive
a benefit or an allowance from the Government.
Motion agreed to.
Bill to be reported without amendment presently.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Such full recognition. I rise to
speak to Part 5 of the Taxation (Annual Rate s, Returns Filing, and Remedial Matters)
5732 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc.) Bill 26 Sep 2012
Bill. I think it is probably appropriate, after such a pause in the proceedings, to remind
members what Part 5 of this bill contains. The bill as a whole, we know, is essentially
tidying up a range of tax measures. Labour will  ultimately support it.  There is little to
disagree with in the bill. There are some things that we think are fairer than others, but
on balance this bill is aimed at ensuring that loopholes in the tax system are tidied up. It
does nothing adventurous. It certainly does not introduce any pro-growth tax measures.
As we come to this part of the bill, we see the provisions in clause 154,
“Contribution rate”—that will give effect to the changes in KiwiSaver that are promoted
in this bill. They are very modest change s; certainly changes that are in the right
direction. Labour welcomes National’s road to Damascus experience on KiwiSaver. It is
far from a universal scheme, the kind of scheme that we would need to see our economy
grow. We know we need more  savings. We know we need  pro-growth tax policy. We
know we need proper monetary policy that would make sure our export industries are
supported.
This Government seems to be firmly and actively pursuing polic ies that involve it
sitting on its hands rather than actually ma king changes that would support business. It
talks a big game, but we see again in this legi slation very little change. It is designed to
maintain the status quo, to ensure that new loopholes are not seen or spotted or
exploited. That effort we must  commend, but we must also  note that there is no real
change of any significant proportion that is going to make our economy run better than
it is now. That is why we know that many New Zealanders are finding times tough.
They are disappointed in the efforts made  by Mr Key. Even those who supported him
are now saying that they are disappointed, they feel let down, and the economy is not
growing, so we understand their need to let ou t those feelings, those of us who have a
different vision, who believe th at the Government can do something to create jobs, and
who believe that positive things can be done—as opposed to this Government, which
just says “no”, “can’t”, and “won’t”, and will not change.
Our Government, a Labour Government in th e future, would make the changes that
would grow the economy. We would be more vigorous in our approach to KiwiSaver.
The change proposed here in clause 154, “Contri bution rate”, is: “In section 64(1)(a), in
the words before the subparagraphs, ‘2%’ is replaced by ‘3%’.” This is the big change
in this part of the bill—2 percent is replaced by 3 percent.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: And it’s reversing one the other way.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: My colleague is quite right. The Hon David Cunliffe points
out that this is a reverse of a change. Th is is the reverse of a change that this
Government made.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Go big, National.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It is a timid reverse. It is a flip-flop, but it is—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: It’s a half reverse.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It is a flop, I guess. This flip is in the right direction. The
Government cut the minimum contribution rates for employees and employers to 2
percent. The Government is the reason that this  2 percent is in the legislation in the first
place. The rate had been progressively raised  to an 8 percent of gross income default
rate for employees by 2011, and a 4 percent default rate for employers. But this
Government took it and capped the em ployer’s superannuation contribution tax
exemption at 2 percent, wher e it was 4 percent. So the Government took it from 4
percent to 2 percent, and now it is taking it from 2 percent back up to 3 percent.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Flip-flop.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Whoa, there we go. It is a flip -flop. It is progress. It is
reversing out of a change it has made, but it is hardly vi sionary stuff. It is hardly
visionary stuff. It is what we have come to expect from this Government.
26 Sep 2012 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc.) Bill 5733

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: It’s damaging.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It is the kind of thing that we have come to expect. It is
actually damaging. My colleague Rajen Prasad points out that this is actually damaging
to confidence in the scheme, this kind of trading. This kind of change does erode
confidence in the scheme. It follows along similar lines.
The Government also previously discont inued the fee subsidy of $40 per annum.
Again, it shows that it does not really have  confidence in the scheme. Well, it does.
Maybe it has a little bit more  now. Maybe it has 3 percent confidence rather than 2
percent. It has got that little bit more c onfidence. We could say that it has 50 percent
more confidence than it had before, but it is half of what it was previously, when it was
4 percent.
We see a Government that is switching around with small numbers in this part of the
bill. It is trying to address KiwiSaver. It is certainly a move in the right direction, but it
is not bold enough. It will not change the fundame ntals. It is not going to be the savings
policy that cracks it, that reverses this  trend—this increased  unemployment, the
thousand people a week leaving for Australia , and the worst economic record of any
Government in 50 years. These are not th e changes that will actually make that
difference.
If we move further through Part 5 we ha ve the clauses on unsuccessful software
development, and we see that these are design ed to ensure that people feel comfortable
investing in software development and ar e not placed in a position where they are
carrying too much risk and are then unable to make the confident business decisions
they need to make to develop new technologies that will take our country forward.
Interestingly, there has been, no doubt, so me confidence eroded in that sector
recently with the Government’s spying ille gally, we understand, on Kim Dotcom as he
went about his software development busine ss in his own private home. So there is a
certain contradiction in here. We see the Government’s actions on the one hand dealing
in an illegal way with a resident of New Zealand wh o is going about software
development, and then on the other hand in this bill we have a measure designed to
encourage software development. You know, we  are seeing a little bi t of tinkering here
and there. We will see the Government, no doubt , reverse this decision in a wee while.
We would not be surprised—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Half.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —or half reversing it, as it did with KiwiSaver. It will
probably say that mildly successful softwa re development will develop some kind of
bonus, but completely unsuccessful will not.
We will see some amendment in due course if it is consistent in its inconsistency—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Asset sales.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —but there is not much more in here than tinkering. Maggie
Barry is suggesting that we bring asset sale s into this debate because her Government
wants to sell off the assets, and 80 percent of  New Zealanders oppose that. In this bill I
do not see a relevance to asset sales, other than perhaps, I guess, we might see software
development as developing new assets, the kind s of assets that might be profitable and,
therefore, something the Government might like to hock off if it owned any share in
them, if it was to be consistent. But, again, we are seeing an inconsistent Government
that is tinkering through this bill.
Clause 165 deals with livestock valuation, and I would be interested if the Minister in
the chair can explain, because I am just no t certain, whether this is relevant to the
provisions and changes around put ting livestock into one cla ss, either as capital or
revenue items, in different years in order to—

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: They’re already capital.
5734 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc.) Bill 26 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —change the tax treatment. That may have been covered
previously. Mr Bennett is shaking his head. I am  sure he will take a call and explain in
due course whether clause 165 has any relevance to that m easure, because we have not
heard anything from the Minister in the chair yet.
Clause 170, in Part 5, talks about certain re pairs to fishing boats. I speculated in a
previous call about wh ether that might also be expande d to cabbage boats, and whether
there are any repairs provisions in respect of  cabbage boats. But we are not quite sure
what cabbage boats are. We know that Mr Banks is fond of referring to them. He is fond
of discussing cabbage boats coming down rivers , and whether he was in the last one or
not—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Not from watching fireworks.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Well, you would not watch fireworks, my colleague Megan
Woods explains, because it would be a dange rous place, and then you might need this
provision for repairs to fishing boats or ca bbage boats, as the case may be. We know
John Key would probably not have been in th at cabbage boat that went down the river
where the fireworks were let off, because he  seems to not know—he tells us today that
Kim Dotcom was a resident of New Zealand. Finally—

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It was not that long ago that New
Zealanders were told by th e National Party to “Wave goodbye  to higher taxes, not your
loved ones.” Does anyone remember that? Do you know what? Natio nal lied. It lied.
What have we had since then? We have had the income gap with Australia widen from
30 percent to 35 percent. We have had the numbers of young New Zealanders—

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I delayed, somewhat,
on the basis that you were going to pull up the unparliamentary comment by that
member. I would ask that you do so now and that he withdraw it.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I was actually thinking about it at
the time. The member knows that you cannot us e the word “lie”, because it actually
reflects on all of the House. I ask the member to desist.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Mr Chairperson, I certainl y take your guidance on that
matter, notwithstanding the fact that it was a factual statement, and the delivery—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! To the member on my right,
you cannot use a live microphone. I just ask the member to go straight to the debate.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: There is no doubt that New Zealanders have not waved
goodbye to higher taxes. That is clear from  this bill, the Ta xation (Annual Rates,
Returns Filing, and Remedial Matters) Bill, which deals with GST, because GST went
up, not down, for all New Zealanders. The tax package of which it was part, which was
promised to be fiscally neutral, was not . I am not sure what  you call it when you
campaign on moving in one direction and th en you do the exact opposite. It is, should
we say, an anomaly, a discontinuity, an untruth, perhaps, in the eye of the beholder.
This bill shows not the ineptitude of the current Government, not the abject failure of
the current Government, but the errant tim idity of this Government. Surrounded by lay-
offs from manufacturing plants each and every week; surrounded by unemployment that
is going up, not down; surrounded by a median in come that has fallen 3 percent since it
took office—
House resumed.
The Chairperson reported the National Wa r Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering
Bill without amendment; the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget
Measures) Amendment Bill without amendment, and that the Committee had divided it
26 Sep 2012 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc.) Bill 5735
into seven bills; progress on the Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing, and Remedial
Matters) Bill; and no progress on the Legislation Bill.
Report adopted.
The House adjourned at 9.57 p.m.

WEDNESDAY, 26 SEPTEMBER 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
Australia—Joint Committee on the National Broadband Network, Commonwealth 
Parliament 
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House 
that the Joint Committee on the Nationa l Broadband Network Committee from the 
Parliament of Australia, led by the Chair, Robe rt Oakeshott, is present in the gallery. I 
am sure that members would wish that the delegation be welcomed. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Dotcom Case—Government Communications Security Bureau Actions 
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by all his statements in relation to Kim Dotcom and the inquiry into the actions of 
the Government Communications Security Bureau? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I stand by my full statements in the context 
in which they were given. 
David Shearer: When did the Government Communi cations Security Bureau begin 
surveillance of Kim Dotcom, and when did it realise it was acting illegally? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I think the memorandum spells out exactly when that work 
began—if the member gives me a moment. It was 16 December 2011, and it ended on 
20 January 2012. The Government Communicati ons Security Bureau recognised the 
error a few days before it told me—I think it was about 5 to 7 days before it told me. 
David Shearer : Who first told him of the Gove rnment Communications Security 
Bureau’s illegal surveillance, and approximately what date was that? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : It was Monday, 17 September when the Government 
Communications Security Bureau came over to advise me there had been an error. 
David Shearer: Is he aware of any involvement by staff from the Department of the 
Prime Minister and Cabinet, the SIS, or the National Assessments Bureau in the 
Dotcom case; if so, what involvement was that? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am not sure about the latter two, the SIS and the National 
Assessments Bureau. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet may have been 
advised. I do not know that—I would have to  go and check that—but it is possible it 
would have known in that period when I was told on Monday the 17th.  
David Shearer: Did he receive any advice from those agencies in the past 12 months 
in relation to the Kim Dotcom case? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Not in relation to this issue. I was informed of that only on 17 
September. Whether there was earlier advice on extradition and ot her matters, I am not 
sure. I do not think so. 
David Shearer: Given that the ministerial certificate signed by Bill English said that 
the Kim Dotcom communication intercepts “w ould likely prejudice the security of New 
Zealand”, does he feel he should have been told well before by either Bill English or his 
own department? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No. It is important to unde rstand what the ministerial 
certificate is. The ministerial certificate is essentially a suppression order that was on the 
basis of an application by Kim Dotcom’s legal team to release the name of the 
5648 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Sep 2012 
Government Communications Security Bureau’s activity. It is not normal practice for us 
to do that. So, because the bureau believed it had acted lawfully, it asked the Acting 
Prime Minister to sign the ministerial certific ate, which avoided it having to make that 
public statement. 
David Shearer: Does he think he was providing pr oper, democratic oversight of his 
agency when he did not receive advice of  the Government Communications Security 
Bureau involvement in the Dotcom case in the past 12 months? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes. It would be quite inappropriate for me to be involved in a 
police raid, and if this member wants to one day be Prime Mini ster and direct the 
police—well, that is a pretty interesting way he is going to go. It is— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That is sufficient. 
Economic Growth—Sustainable Growth and Higher Incomes 
2. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What progress is the 
Government making to ensure New Zeala nd’s economic growth is sustainable and 
supports jobs and higher incomes? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: I can report that the Government is making good progress. Since 2008 we 
have been working hard through our br oad-based economic programme to support 
business competitiveness in areas such as the tax system, exporting, skills, innovation, 
infrastructure, capital markets, and resources. We are seeing good results. The economy 
is now growing moderately well, compared with the rest of th e world. A net 57,000 
more New Zealanders now have jobs than 2 years ago. Household saving is positive, for 
the first time in more than a decade, and total goods and serv ices exported have 
increased 15 percent over the last 2 years. 
Hon Tau Henare : How is the New Zealand economy performing, according to the 
latest official gross domestic product statistics? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Statistics New Zealand last week, of course, reported the 
gross domestic product data for the June quarter 2012. They showed that the New 
Zealand economy grew 0.6 percent in the 3 months to 30 June, and growth for the first 6 
months of the year was 1.6 percent. The qua rterly growth was re asonably broad-based, 
including agriculture up 4.7 per cent, construction up 3.3 percen t, transport, postal, and 
warehousing up 2.7 percent, and manufacturi ng up 0.8 percent. New Zealand’s annual 
growth rate of 2.6 percent to June 2012 wa s the highest growth rate since 2007, before 
the domestic recession, the Canterbury earthquakes, and the global financial crisis. 
Hon Tau Henare : How does current progress in building a more productive and 
competitive economy compare with the situation in late 2008? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : New Zealanders can be reassured that New Zealand’s 
current economic situation is much healthier than it wa s in late 2008. Annual economic 
growth is up to 2.6 percent, compared with negative 1.7 percent in December 2008. The 
number of people on the unemployment benef it has declined from a peak of 93,000 at 
the height of the global financial crisis to 58,000 in July of this year. The household 
savings rate is now in positive territory, compared with negative 3 percent in 2008. The 
cost of living is flat, with CPI inflation only 1 percent in the year to  June 2012, 
compared with 5.1 percent in 2008. The New Z ealand sharemarket is at a 4-year high, 
and the average floating mortgage interest rate  is 5.7 percent, compar ed with almost 11 
percent in 2008. This all shows that New Z ealand is in pretty good shape, compared 
with most other developed countries. 
Hon Tau Henare : What reports has he seen on new projects that would create 
further investment and jobs? 
26 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5649 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The Minister sees reports ev ery day, and just yesterday he 
has seen a report on a project in regard to the Bathurst  Resources escarpment mines 
project near Westport. This project would apparently immediately create 225 new jobs 
and incomes for workers and families on the West Coast. Unfortunately, it is being held 
up by ongoing litigation. Yesterday the Minister saw a report calling for objectors to the 
mine to withdraw their appeal s and consider the economic futu re of the West Coast. It 
prevailed upon various groups to join the call.  As yet, the Minister has seen no reports 
that the Labour Party, the local Labour MP, the Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and 
Manufacturing Union, or the Greens will support— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I think the answer has gone on quite long enough. 
Hon David Parker : Given the 8 percent decline in exports in the year to August, 
announced by Statistics New Zealand just t oday, and Treasury’s prediction that our 
external deficit will get even worse, when will he accept that his plan is deficient, 
costing exports and jobs, and what is sustainable about that? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I would point out to the member that New Zealand’s 
exports have grown substantially since his Government left office, and I would point 
out that the balance of payments deficit, the external deficit, is considerably lower than 
when his Government left office. But I s uppose it is all relative. We know that this 
Government is a better economic manager. 
Hon David Parker : When exports are declining, lo cal businesses are closing, and 
thousands of Kiwis are losing their jobs and heading to Australia, why does he sit on his 
hands and pretend there is nothing he can do about our inflated currency? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I think I hear the printi ng presses cranking up on the 
Labour Party side, but I would point out to th e member that he is incorrect. The decline 
in manufacturing jobs in New Zealand occurred under the previous Government and 
through the global financial cris is. Over the last 2 years the number of manufacturing 
jobs has actually grown.

Parole—Reduction in Unnecessary Hearings 
5. IAN McKELVIE (National—Rangitīkei) to the Minister of Justice: What steps 
is the Government taking to reduce the st ress on victims caused by unnecessary parole 
hearings? 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Minister of Justice) : I have today introduced legislation 
to implement the Government’s post-election action plan to reduce the number of 
unnecessary parole hearings where the offender has little prospect of release. This will 
help to reduce the stress caused to victim s by having to attend unnecessary parole 
hearings and relive their traumatic experiences when the offender is not genuinely ready 
for parole. It is estimated that these cha nges will mean 800 fewer parole hearings each 
year. 
Ian McKelvie: How will the changes to the parole regime operate? 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS : The Parole Amendment Bill increases the time between 
parole hearings from once every year to once every 2 years, and for those serving 
indeterminate sentences or sentences of 10  or more years the maximum time between 
parole hearings increases from 3 years to 5 years. Inmates will be encouraged to comply 
with offender plans, which will have agreed  goals that aim to reduce the likelihood of 
future offending. Hearing dates will be aligned with the completion of milestones. Early 
hearings can be held for offenders who achieve early completion of goals.

What difference do social workers make in  protecting our most vulnerable children 
from abuse and neglect?

Youth and Family social workers deal with more than 400 notifi cations of abuse and 
neglect every day in New Zealand. Social workers often bear the brunt of criticism 
when things go wrong, but the fact is they do the job because they care, and every day 
they do the best they can to protect New Zealand. Ultimately, they save children’s lives.

Fuel Efficiency—Heavy Vehicle Fuel Efficiency Programme 
12. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney)  to the Minister of Energy and 
Resources: What progress has the Government ma de on promoting fuel efficiency in 
heavy road vehicles? 
Hon PHIL HEATLEY (Minister of Energy and Resources): Last week I launched 
the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority’s Heavy Vehicle Fuel Efficiency 
programme, which will help fleet operators cut their fuel bills by 10 percent on average, 
with some achieving savings of up to 20 per cent. If all heavy ve hicle fleets in New 
Zealand reduce their fuel bills by 10 per cent, nationwide savi ngs could total $130 
million each year. This initiative will help ou r vehicle fleet to become significantly 
more fuel efficient, with the wider economy and the environment reaping the rewards. 
Mark Mitchell: How important is the heavy fleet sector for fuel efficiency? 
Hon PHIL HEATLEY : Transport makes up around 40 percent of New Zealand’s 
energy use, and New Zealand’s heavy vehicle fleet of 127,000 makes up about a fifth of 
this. At an individual company level, a fleet of 25 trucks using 1 million litres of fuel 
annually, which is not unusual, could realistically make savings of $130,000 per annum. 
With a very competitive industry and with small profit margins, these savings are very 
significant to the bottom line of companies.

robust one for the former and a slightly simple r one for the latter. We will tease that out 
at the Commerce Committee. It certainly seem s reasonable. We think the pre-vetting of 
applicants first up is good. For those organisa tions or those companies that we may not 
want to come into New Zealand—because realis tically, even if they put a lot of money 
into resource consents under this legisla tion, they are not going to get through—it is 
good to signal upfront that that is not likel y to happen. Again, at the select committee 
we will have a look at the details of that, but I take on board the assurances from the 
Minister of Energy and Resources  that that does not replac e the other processes in the 
piece of legislation.  
26 Sep 2012 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 5681 
The areas where we have concerns are ar ound the sharing of responsibility for 
decision making on concessions on conserva tion land. This is something that we 
flagged right back when the Government first announced it. And, let us be honest, it 
was a knee-jerk reaction to the schedule 4 mining issue where the Government had to 
back down, so as a kind of countermeasure it said “Well, now for concessions for 
mining on Department of Conservation land it is going to be half-shared by the Minister 
of Energy and Resources and half-shared by the Minister of Conservation.”, whereas 
previously the Minister of Conservation ha d sole responsibility for that. There has 
always been a contention in Crown mineral law that mining is treated separately from 
every other economic activity. I mean, tourism creates jobs in New Zealand as well, and 
tourism has to get concessions on Depart ment of Conservation land. But they go 
through a process under the Conservation Act th at involves the public and that involves 
notification, and mining has never had to  go through that pr ocess because it goes 
through the Crown Minerals Act. That has always been a point of contention.  
That is why the Minister of Conservation, when it came to the issue of Bathurst, 
which members have been talking about, sa id “Well, the Government is going to 
publicly notify these concessions  for mining.” I notice in this  legislation that it has not 
gone that far. What it says is that now th e Minister of Energy and Resources and the 
Minister of Conservation will  have a shared res ponsibility for deciding whether or not 
these concessions for mining go to public no tification. That is not what was promised, 
and I take on board what my colleague Dami en O’Connor said, which is that if the 
Government wants to take the heat out of some of these projects, then do not make 
promises and then not keep them—do not s hut people out of a process. That is a 
genuinely serious comment. A lot of what has happened around the Denniston issue has 
been that a promise was made and then not kept . So that is our concern in terms of that 
sharing of responsibility.  
What I have been pleased about, as the Minist er has indicated, is th at he is prepared 
to try to work with the Opposition to find a way through. This has been a line call for us 
on this piece of legislation. There is a lot in  here that is really good—that sharing of 
responsibility, and the introduc tion of an economic test for mining that does not exist 
for any other commercial activity. Why should tourism not get an economic benefit test

unfairness, and there is genuine concern in the community. But what we are here to say

EUGENIE SAGE (Green) : The Green Party is opposin g this Crown Minerals 
(Permitting and Crown Land) Bill because it makes a fundamental attack on 
conservation legislation. In the schedule 4 debate in 2010, when 50,000 people marched 
down Queen Street in support of protection of national parks and not opening them up 
to mining, the National Party sought to get out of the can of worms it had opened by
