bill substantially weakens the process for considering access applications on 
conservation land because of its provision for those decisions to be made jointly by the 
Minister of Conservation a nd the Minister of Energy and Resources and because of the 
introduction of the economic benefits test.  
We have seen this week that Ministers Joyce and English were  putting pressure on 
conservation groups and environmental interests that are quite legitimately involved in a 
case before the Environment Court on the resource consent applications for the Bathurst 
Resources mine on the Denniston Plateau. The Ministers have been putting pressure on 
those objectors to withdraw. It is obvious th at the Ministers and others on the National 
benches have not been to Denniston, are not aware of the outstanding landscape and 
biodiversity values on the Denni ston Plateau, and are not aw are of the significance of 
those coal measure ecosystems, which are pr otected as conservation land. The risk is 
that if you have a joint deci sion-making power, as the bill provides, you w ill have the 
Minister of Energy and Res ources and his views overriding those of the Minister of 
Conservation and the Department of Conserva tion. We have already seen that with the 
Māui’s dolphin decision and th e Minister for Primary Industr ies and that department’s 
views overriding the Department of Conserva tion’s views about th e need to protect 
Māui’s dolphins. Where you get that join t decision-making power, the user 
department’s views prevail.  
The other major defect in the bill is the way in which it amends section 61 of the 
Crown Minerals Act. It is section 61 that sets out the matters that the appropriate 
Minister must have regard to in cons idering whether to agree to an access 
arrangement—that is, the obj ectives of any Act under whic h the land is administered, 
26 Sep 2012 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 5695 
and the purpose for which the land is held  by the Crown. The bill, in clause 31, 
introduces an economic benefits test, and requires the Ministers to consider “the 
economic and other benefits of the proposed  activity in relation to which the access 
arrangement is sought”. That is a fundamental weakening of  conservation legislation, 
because it means that the Ministers will be weighing up the economic benefits as well as 
the conservation purpose for which the land is held.  
We know under this Government that economic benefits always triumph over nature, 
and that the short-term gains of opening an open-cast coalmine on the Denniston 
Plateau would potentially triumph over the biod iversity values. That is despite the fact 
that the Denniston Plateau is becoming increasingly popu lar as a mountain biking 
destination and as a place where people go to  recreate and to look at the outstanding 
landscapes—the rock tors, the gullies, and the stunted vegetation—that are special to 
coal measure ecosystems. By introducing this  economic benefit test, that will override 
conservation values. That is why everyone, particularly conservation groups and anyone 
concerned about the future of conservation land, should be concerned about this bill, 
because it cuts across the protective provisions that exist in the Conservation Act.  
Yes, the public may get the opportunity to make a submission on access 
arrangements if the proposed mine is significant in the Ministers’ opinions, but this 
weakening of the application of the Conser vation Act potentially means that it will be 
much easier for those mining access applications to be approved. That is one of the 
reasons the Green Party is opposing this bill, because it is an attack on our conservation 
legislation.

saying, as I believe my colleagues have at othe r stages of this bill , that the Green Party

provide New Zealanders and overseas visitors with a dedicated space in which to reflect 
on the loss and sacrifice of lif e in numerous armed conflicts, to pay respect to the dead, 
to contemplate the causes for which those conflicts were fought, and also, importantly, 
to consider the cause of peace and to refl ect on how future armed conflicts may be 
avoided. It also would provide a haven of much-needed green space within the busy 
environs of the capital city.

some of the amendments made at the sele ct committee, because of our fundamental 
concerns about the extraordinary powers granted by the legislation.

Industrial Relations Committee, which I sat in on for the duration of this bill. I think the 
first point to note about that select committee process is that it was an extremely 
constrained one and very challenging for th e committee to do its work within the time 
frame, and, indeed, for the officials to do th e work within the tim e frame allocated, and

the committee did work well, and I enjoyed my experience on the committee. 
I am pleased to say that some of the amendments that the committee has made are 
minor improvements to the bill—for exampl e, the adoption of changes recommended

accountability of the Order in Council proce ss by making sure that Ministers have to 
explore every other available option releva nt before moving to making Orders in 
Council, and, indeed, to beef up and improve the community forum and improve the 
number of times that that community forum is delegated to meet.

unfortunately, the fundamental concerns that  the Green Party has with the legislation

scrutiny. We in the Green Party are very concerned about the pr ecedent that these

Committee, which expressed concern that if we put aside the rule of law in the case of

Measures) Amendment Bill. What Part 1 of this bill does is allow for four substantive 
10 percent increases in the excise duty on tobacco products. This is being done in the 
name of harm reduction, to reduce the harm caused by tobacco smoking in New 
Zealand. It is being done in a wa y that, as has been discussed in earlier readings of this 
bill, actually follows the evidence for using tax increases or price increases to reduce the 
prevalence of smoking in a much stronger way than previous increases have done. That 
is because it allows for four successive increases in price. What the evidence tells us is 
that each time we have a price increase, then associated with that is a spike in quitting 
activity, whether that be people contacting or ganisations like Quitline, whether that be 
acquiring nicotine replacement treatments—or  a whole host of quitting activities. We 
also know that as a result of those quitti ng activities many people do remain tobacco-
free as a result of those quit attempts, although the nature of addiction being what it is, 
many people also go back to using cigarettes and other tobacco products after those quit 
attempts. But what we also know is that ther e is a brief period of activity after each 
increase, which then tails off, and we retu rn to a steady level of tobacco consumption, 
albeit hopefully lower than what it was pr evious to the increase. So with these 
consecutive increases, what we should then see are consecutive periods of quitting 
activity from people who are currently using tobacco, and they will assist in progressing 
New Zealand towards the goal of being smoke-free by 2025.  
But it is important to also note that this, being a tax increase, does generate additional 
revenue for the Government. Treasury estimat es that this legisl ation will raise an 
additional $528 million for the Government over the next 4 years. What I found 
interesting is that for a pi ece of legislation that the Government has proposed in the 
name of health and in the name of harm reduction, this bill went not to the Health 
Committee but to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and, in fact, the reports, the 
regulatory impact statement, and the departmental report were prepared by Treasury not 
by the Ministry of Health. That is more appropriate for a bill that is designed purely as a 
revenue-gathering exercise, rather than an exercise in improving the health and well-
being of New Zealanders. The chair of the Health Committee is looking at me a little bit 
perplexed and is perhaps concerned that I might be suggesting this is not a health 
measure and is, in fact, just a revenue-gat hering exercise. I do not believe that, Mr 
Hutchison. I do know that this is being do ne with the best intentions—the right 
intentions. But it does also  raise money for the Govern ment, and it comes at an 
interesting time.  
It is interesting that the G overnment has chosen now, rather  than the year before, or 
the year before that, or even going back to the days when National was in Opposition, to 
support a bill like this. Of course, what we  do know is that the Government has been 
having a lot of trouble raising the revenue it requires, because the economy is so 
sluggish at the moment. So this does have a positive benefit for a Government that is 
having a lot of trouble in its economic manage ment at the moment. It is having some 
difficult getting the economy moving along. This measure does have an additional 
benefit for the Government in that it does raise some more  revenue. That, of course, 
then begs the question of what the Government  ought to do with that revenue. It is true 
that there are a number of m easures that the Government could be undertaking in order 
5708 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 26 Sep 2012 
to further tackle the prevalence of tobacco smoking, and to further advance New 
Zealand towards that goal of being smoke-f ree by 2025, that, in fact, would be a very, 
very good use for this money.  
There is a range of things that the money being raised from the sale of tobacco could 
be used for, whether it be through GS T, and whether it be through excise tax. 
Obviously, there is the expend iture on the treatment of peop le who have diseases that 
are related to smoking. There is , of course, tobacco. We know that tobacco is related to 
all the big four killers—not just the big four k illers, but the big four creators of cost in 
the health system—cardiovascular disease, di abetes, respiratory disease, and, of course, 
cancer, which is well documented. Of course, a lot of the money raised from the duties, 
excises, and GST on tobacco products needs to be used to pay for those treatments. It 
also needs to be used to boost the health promotion activities that the Government ought 
to be carrying out in order to convince people to not start smoking in the first place, and 
also to quit.  
Of course, what we know is that one of the other initiatives that has a strong evidence 
base behind it is social marketing, which encourages people to quit. In fact, if that social 
marketing was aligned to these tax increases, it would have an additional effect in 
encouraging people to give up smoking. Unfortuna tely, the truth is that the Government 
has reduced its spending on those social marketing initiatives, despite the fact that it is 
increasing its revenue from the sale of tobacco. 
There is a third area that needs to be cove red as well, and this, perhaps, does not get 
as much consideration or debate in the public . That is the fact th at people who do get a 
disease that is related to smoking of tobacco products are less productive. They are less 
able to work. They, therefore, pay less ta x. So there is a burden on the New Zealand 
taxpayer because of that loss of productivity that is related to tobacco smoking as well, 
and that ought to be covered off by the money raised through tobacco taxation too.  
There is an important question that the Government ought to answer: what is it 
planning to do with this a dditional money? Is this ju st making up for its economic 
failures? Is this just a way of filling the hole created by its unaffordable income tax cuts, 
as we have seen with the range of other levies and costs placed on the New Zealand 
taxpayer through indirect taxation that does not come through income tax, and making 
up for that loss of revenue from income tax, or will this money be used to get us closer 
to that goal of making New Zealand smoke-f ree by 2025? I would appreciate an answer 
from the Minister in the ch air, the Minister of Ener gy and Resources, on those 
questions, because I think they are important questions.  
People do accept that increasing the revenue that the Government takes from tobacco 
is an effective method for reducing the harm caused by tobacco, but it does have an 
impact, particularly on low-income people w ho are addicted to tobacco products. And I 
note that Treasury actually acknowledges in its regulatory impact statement that the 
nature of addiction is that even if a product beco mes more unaffordable, people may 
continue using it because they are addicted to  it, and they do not necessarily make what 
most people might consider a logical decision about their use of that product. So given 
that that is the situation, it would be fair  for the Government to do more in terms of 
supporting people to quit, encouraging people to  quit, and making sure that the types of 
replacement therapies, social  marketing, and all the othe r things that go along with 
encouraging less use of tobacco amongst the population of New Zealand would all be 
good things to be funded out of this money. So I do ask the Minister, if he feels inclined 
to get to his feet, to answer those questions on Part 1 of this bill.

for all smokers would not include the tobacco  tax increase. Rather, it has taken the 
approach that only those who receive some fo rm of income from the Government will 
be affected. That is why the Labour Party is  certainly happy to se e the separation of 
these bills, because we want to be able to vo te for the parts of this bill that we think 
make sense.  
26 Sep 2012 Customs & Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget) Amdt Bill 5731 
We agree that increasing tobacco taxation is one way of reducing the harm caused by 
tobacco. We suspect that the Government’s real motivation behind doing that is to make 
up for its lost revenue, but we do appreciate the perhaps unintended consequence for the 
Government of doing so—that it will reduce to bacco-related harm. So we want to be 
able to vote for that aspect of the bill, bu t we actually appreciat e that this amendment 
will allow us to vote against those measures that we think are rather insidious and create 
just one more division between people who receive income from the Government and 
other New Zealanders. That is certainly what this Government’s approach has been over 
the last few weeks: to drive that wedge be tween some New Zealanders and others as 
hard as it can. It wants to see people fighting amongst themselves. It wants to see people 
pointing the finger of blame at the victims of  poverty rather than trying to do something 
about it. This bill, in its own small way, has been found out t onight as being part of that 
Government programme to continue to discriminate against anybody—anybody. It is a 
broad brush in this bill; even the poor vetera ns are getting hit with this bill. So we 
certainly support— 
Denis O’Rourke: Superannuitants. 
IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY: And the superannuitants—you are absolutely right. The 
superannuitants, the families who receive Working for Families—a whole range of 
people are going to be unnecessari ly discriminated against with  this legislation. So it is 
good that this bill will be separated out into  its component parts by this Supplementary 
Order Paper in the name of the Hon Tarian a Turia. That will give the right-minded 
parties in this Chamber the oppor tunity to vote for those asp ects of the legislation that 
will do good, and against those aspects of the legislation that will do harm.  
It is a noble idea to ensure that the excise tax increase results in an increase in real 
terms in the cost of tobacco, but it is not noble at all—it is as far from noble as is 
humanly possible to be—to determine that one  group of New Zealanders will be hit by 
that methodology and others will escape from it.  
The Labour Opposition is very happy to s upport this Supplementary Order Paper in 
the name of the Hon Tariana Turia. We think it will be useful—it will be quite useful—
because it actually will allow Parliament to reveal what so me of these measures really 
are, what their true intended purpose is, and will give Opposition parties the opportunity 
to cast their votes accordingly. As I have said, I want to signal that tomorrow during the 
third reading debate on these bills, as th ey will be by then, the Labour Opposition will 
certainly be voting against those measures th at discriminate against people who receive 
a benefit or an allowance from the Government.  
Motion agreed to.

The CHAIRPERSON (H V Ross Robertson) : When this bill was last being 
considered, we had reached Part 5. The Hon Damien O’Connor had the call. He has 25 
seconds remaining, if he so wishes. I cal l the honourable member the Rev. Dr David 
Clark. 
Dr DAVID CLARK (Labour—Dunedin North) : Such full recognition. I rise to 
speak to Part 5 of the Taxation (Annual Rate s, Returns Filing, and Remedial Matters) 
5732 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc.) Bill 26 Sep 2012 
Bill. I think it is probably appropriate, after such a pause in the proceedings, to remind 
members what Part 5 of this bill contains. The bill as a whole, we know, is essentially 
tidying up a range of tax measures. Labour will  ultimately support it.  There is little to 
disagree with in the bill. There are some things that we think are fairer than others, but 
on balance this bill is aimed at ensuring that loopholes in the tax system are tidied up. It 
does nothing adventurous. It certainly does not introduce any pro-growth tax measures.  
As we come to this part of the bill, we see the provisions in clause 154, 
“Contribution rate”—that will give effect to the changes in KiwiSaver that are promoted 
in this bill. They are very modest change s; certainly changes that are in the right 
direction. Labour welcomes National’s road to Damascus experience on KiwiSaver. It is 
far from a universal scheme, the kind of scheme that we would need to see our economy 
grow. We know we need more  savings. We know we need  pro-growth tax policy. We 
know we need proper monetary policy that would make sure our export industries are 
supported.  
This Government seems to be firmly and actively pursuing polic ies that involve it 
sitting on its hands rather than actually ma king changes that would support business. It 
talks a big game, but we see again in this legi slation very little change. It is designed to 
maintain the status quo, to ensure that new loopholes are not seen or spotted or 
exploited. That effort we must  commend, but we must also  note that there is no real 
change of any significant proportion that is going to make our economy run better than 
it is now. That is why we know that many New Zealanders are finding times tough. 
They are disappointed in the efforts made  by Mr Key. Even those who supported him 
are now saying that they are disappointed, they feel let down, and the economy is not 
growing, so we understand their need to let ou t those feelings, those of us who have a 
different vision, who believe th at the Government can do something to create jobs, and 
who believe that positive things can be done—as opposed to this Government, which 
just says “no”, “can’t”, and “won’t”, and will not change.  
Our Government, a Labour Government in th e future, would make the changes that 
would grow the economy. We would be more vigorous in our approach to KiwiSaver. 
The change proposed here in clause 154, “Contri bution rate”, is: “In section 64(1)(a), in 
the words before the subparagraphs, ‘2%’ is replaced by ‘3%’.” This is the big change 
in this part of the bill—2 percent is replaced by 3 percent. 
Hon David Cunliffe: And it’s reversing one the other way. 
Dr DAVID CLARK : My colleague is quite right. The Hon David Cunliffe points 
out that this is a reverse of a change. Th is is the reverse of a change that this 
Government made. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Go big, National. 
Dr DAVID CLARK: It is a timid reverse. It is a flip-flop, but it is— 
Hon David Cunliffe: It’s a half reverse. 
Dr DAVID CLARK : It is a flop, I guess. This flip is in the right direction. The 
Government cut the minimum contribution rates for employees and employers to 2 
percent. The Government is the reason that this  2 percent is in the legislation in the first 
place. The rate had been progressively raised  to an 8 percent of gross income default 
rate for employees by 2011, and a 4 percent default rate for employers. But this 
Government took it and capped the em ployer’s superannuation contribution tax 
exemption at 2 percent, wher e it was 4 percent. So the Government took it from 4 
percent to 2 percent, and now it is taking it from 2 percent back up to 3 percent. 
Dr Rajen Prasad: Flip-flop. 
Dr DAVID CLARK : Whoa, there we go. It is a flip -flop. It is progress. It is 
reversing out of a change it has made, but it is hardly vi sionary stuff. It is hardly 
visionary stuff. It is what we have come to expect from this Government. 
26 Sep 2012 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc.) Bill 5733 
Dr Rajen Prasad: It’s damaging. 
Dr DAVID CLARK : It is the kind of thing that we have come to expect. It is 
actually damaging. My colleague Rajen Prasad points out that this is actually damaging 
to confidence in the scheme, this kind of trading. This kind of change does erode 
confidence in the scheme. It follows along similar lines. 
 The Government also previously discont inued the fee subsidy of $40 per annum. 
Again, it shows that it does not really have  confidence in the scheme. Well, it does. 
Maybe it has a little bit more  now. Maybe it has 3 percent confidence rather than 2 
percent. It has got that little bit more c onfidence. We could say that it has 50 percent 
more confidence than it had before, but it is half of what it was previously, when it was 
4 percent.  
We see a Government that is switching around with small numbers in this part of the 
bill. It is trying to address KiwiSaver. It is certainly a move in the right direction, but it 
is not bold enough. It will not change the fundame ntals. It is not going to be the savings 
policy that cracks it, that reverses this  trend—this increased  unemployment, the 
thousand people a week leaving for Australia , and the worst economic record of any 
Government in 50 years. These are not th e changes that will actually make that 
difference.  
If we move further through Part 5 we ha ve the clauses on unsuccessful software 
development, and we see that these are design ed to ensure that people feel comfortable 
investing in software development and ar e not placed in a position where they are 
carrying too much risk and are then unable to make the confident business decisions 
they need to make to develop new technologies that will take our country forward.  
Interestingly, there has been, no doubt, so me confidence eroded in that sector 
recently with the Government’s spying ille gally, we understand, on Kim Dotcom as he 
went about his software development busine ss in his own private home. So there is a 
certain contradiction in here. We see the Government’s actions on the one hand dealing

development, and then on the other hand in this bill we have a measure designed to 
encourage software development. You know, we  are seeing a little bi t of tinkering here 
and there. We will see the Government, no doubt , reverse this decision in a wee while. 
We would not be surprised— 
Hon David Cunliffe: Half. 
Dr DAVID CLARK : —or half reversing it, as it did with KiwiSaver. It will 
probably say that mildly successful softwa re development will develop some kind of 
bonus, but completely unsuccessful will not.  
 We will see some amendment in due course if it is consistent in its inconsistency—

Dr DAVID CLARK : —but there is not much more in here than tinkering. Maggie
